meta.title: SK Hynix — Kwak Noh-Jung's HBM-leadership memory pure-play through the AI infrastructure cycle
meta.abstract: SK Hynix Inc. is a South Korean memory semiconductor company listed on the Korea Exchange (KRX: 000660). Headquartered in Icheon, South Korea, SK Hynix is the world's second-largest DRAM memory producer (after Samsung Electronics) and one of the principal global NAND flash memory producers. Within the broader SK Group conglomerate the company sits as the principal SK Group semiconductor subsidiary following the 2012 SK Group acquisition of Hynix Semiconductor (then a creditor-controlled distressed company emerging from the 2001-2002 Hynix workout period). The corporate trajectory through 2012-2026 has been substantially shaped by the multi-decade Hynix-and-subsequent-SK-Hynix DRAM business positioning, the broader NAND flash memory business positioning, the 2021 acquisition of the Intel NAND and Solidigm SSD business for approximately USD 9 billion (closed first phase December 2021, full closing December 2025), and more recent strategic positioning as the principal scaled HBM supplier to Nvidia across the HBM3 and HBM3E product cycle providing the principal AI infrastructure cycle positioning. Under CEO Kwak Noh-Jung (since March 2024, succeeding Park Jung-ho who continues as Vice Chairman) the strategic mandate has been the HBM leadership continuation, the broader memory business trajectory, and the broader strategic posture refinement. Fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately KRW 66.2 trillion (~USD 50 billion) reflecting the substantial HBM contribution plus the broader memory cycle recovery.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) posted KRW 23.47 trillion in fiscal 2024 operating profit — a KRW 31 trillion swing from the KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss of fiscal 2023 — on revenue that more than doubled year-on-year to KRW 66.19 trillion (~USD 50 billion). The principal driver was the HBM premium on NVIDIA supply: a structural lead the Icheon, South Korea-headquartered company had accumulated through years of high-bandwidth memory investment before the AI infrastructure build-out became consensus. By fiscal 2025, the trajectory had extended to records: revenue of KRW 97.15 trillion and operating profit of KRW 47.21 trillion, both figures the highest in the company's history. [SK Hynix FY2025 Financial Results](https://news.skhynix.com/sk-hynix-announces-fy25-financial-results/)

SK Hynix is the world's second-largest DRAM producer after Samsung Electronics and one of the principal global NAND flash producers. Its strategic centre, however, has migrated decisively to HBM. As the principal scaled supplier to NVIDIA across HBM3 (H100, H200) and HBM3E (Blackwell B100/B200/GB200), the company held approximately 57 percent of global HBM market revenue through 2025 — reversing the structural Samsung scale advantage that had defined the DRAM duopoly for more than a decade. [Counterpoint Research via NineScrolls](https://ninescrolls.com/news/sk-hynix-q1-2026-record-52-6-trillion-won-revenue-72-operating-margin-m15x-fab)

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung ~~assumed the role in March 2024~~ ==has served as President & CEO since March 2022== after a 30-year SK Hynix career that spanned semiconductor manufacturing and a prior term as President and Chief Production Officer; he holds a Ph.D. in ~~electrical engineering from KAIST~~ ==Materials Engineering from Korea University==. His predecessor, Park Jung-ho, continues as Vice Chairman. Both answer ultimately to SK Group Chairman Choi Tae-won, who controls SK Hynix through SK Inc. and ~~SK Telecom~~ ==SK Square== in the chaebol cross-shareholding structure.

## The Cycle That Made the Case

Fiscal 2023 was the steepest memory cycle downturn in a decade. Post-COVID inventory unwinding collided with the AI-cycle pre-spend gap to produce a KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss — the worst annual result of the modern company's history. Fiscal 2024 was the mirror image: the sharpest single-year recovery on record, driven by HBM premiums that the commodity DRAM market could not replicate.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Operating Profit (KRW T) |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 44.62 | 6.81 |
| 2023 | 32.77 | (7.73) |
| 2024 | 66.19 | 23.47 |
| 2025 | 97.15 | 47.21 |

That momentum ran well into 2026. For Q1 2026, SK Hynix reported revenue of KRW 52.58 trillion (~USD 38.2 billion) — the first quarter in company history above KRW 50 trillion, and up 198 percent year-on-year — with operating profit of KRW 37.61 trillion and a 72 percent operating margin, an all-time high for any reporting period. [StorageNewsletter](https://www.storagenewsletter.com/2026/04/29/sk-hynix-fiscal-1q26-financial-results/) DRAM unit volumes were broadly flat against Q4 2025; the profit expansion was a product-mix effect, with shipments deliberately concentrated in high-margin HBM and high-density server modules.

> "HBM demand required of the company over the next three years far exceeds our supply capacity." — Kim Ki-tae, Vice President, HBM Sales & Marketing, Q1 2026 earnings call. [Seoul Economic Daily](https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/04/23/sk-hynixs-hbm-sells-out-for-3-years-dram-supply-runs-short)

## Solidigm and the NAND Flank

SK Hynix completed phase one of its Intel NAND acquisition on 29 December 2021 — the opening tranche of an approximately USD 9 billion two-phase transaction that transferred Intel's NAND SSD business and Dalian, China fabrication assets into a new US-headquartered subsidiary named Solidigm Technology, operating from ~~San Jose under Rob Crooke, the former Intel SVP who had run the Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group~~ ==Rancho Cordova, California under co-CEOs David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh, appointed in May 2023==. Full close, transferring the remaining wafer-supply intellectual property, ~~was expected by December 2025~~ ==occurred on 27 March 2025 for approximately USD 1.9 billion net of adjustments==. Solidigm positioned SK Hynix in enterprise SSD — serving the same hyperscaler data-centre customers who consume HBM — though the subsidiary's Dalian manufacturing concentration carries a distinct geopolitical exposure that the parent has not resolved.

## The Central Tension

The company's structural question is straightforward to state and difficult to resolve. SK Hynix announced the world's first HBM4 mass-production readiness in September 2025 and achieved what it characterised as "meaningful results" in NVIDIA's HBM4 System-in-Package testing by January 2026. TrendForce reported in March 2026 that both Samsung and SK Hynix had been tapped as sole suppliers for NVIDIA's Rubin platform. [TrendForce, March 2026](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/03/09/news-samsung-sk%E2%80%AFhynix-reportedly-tapped-as-nvidia-rubin-hbm4-suppliers-shipments-could-start-in-march/) Samsung, however, passed both NVIDIA's 10 Gb/s and 11 Gb/s HBM4 qualification tiers, while SK Hynix was still optimising for the higher threshold as of early 2026. Micron's emerging HBM3E share represented a third competitive vector. By April 2026, Digitimes reported that SK Hynix might reduce planned 2026 HBM4 shipments to NVIDIA by 20 to 30 percent amid Vera Rubin platform ramp delays — a reminder that even the structurally advantaged supplier is exposed to its largest customer's product cycle timing. [Digitimes, April 2026](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20260415VL210/sk-hynix-hbm4-shipments-nvidia-rubin.html)

> "For HBM4, just as with HBM3 and HBM3E, we aim for an overwhelming market share." — SK Hynix executive, Q4 2025 earnings call. [Tweaktown](https://www.tweaktown.com/news/109956/sk-hynix-makes-significant-progress-in-nvidias-extensive-hbm4-tests-close-to-mass-supply/index.html)

Whether the 2024-to-2026 profit cycle represents a structural elevation or the sharpest inflection in a long mean-reverting industry remains the central question for any investor holding the name. SK Hynix's HBM lead has compressed the answer considerably — but it has not eliminated it.

chapters.title: From Hyundai Electronics through creditor workout to SK Hynix
chapters.body:
## Hyundai Electronics: Scale as Strategy (1983–1999)

SK Hynix's origins lie not in the semiconductor ambitions of a technology company but in the industrial logic of a Korean conglomerate that believed memory chips were a commodity business best won through sheer manufacturing scale. Hyundai Electronics was established in 1983 as a division of the Hyundai Group, the sprawling chaebol whose portfolio already spanned shipbuilding, construction, and automobiles. The founding premise — that Korea could build world-class DRAM fabs by combining cheap capital, disciplined labour, and relentless capacity investment — proved durable even if the corporate structures that incubated it did not.

Through the late 1980s and 1990s, Hyundai Electronics built successive generations of DRAM fabs, tracking the technology node cadence from the then-dominant 1-micron generation toward the sub-0.25-micron processes that defined the late-decade mainstream. The company was capital-intensive and leverage-dependent in the fashion common to Korean heavy industry, running fabrication operations with debt loads that would have been unusual for Western technology peers but were normalised within the chaebol financial model. By the late 1990s, Hyundai Electronics had established itself as one of a handful of globally scaled DRAM producers alongside Samsung Electronics, Micron Technology, and Germany's Infineon — subscale on margins, formidable on volume.

## The Big Deal and the Breaking Point (1999–2001)

In 1999, the Korean government's post-financial-crisis industrial restructuring programme — the so-called Big Deal — forced a consolidation of the domestic semiconductor industry. LG Semicon, the memory operation of LG Group and the fourth significant Korean DRAM producer, was merged into Hyundai Electronics on terms dictated by the state rather than the market. The transaction added manufacturing capacity, headcount, and intellectual property, but it also added leverage to a company already strained by the late-1990s DRAM price collapse and the aftershocks of the 1997 Asian financial crisis.

The combined entity entered the 2001 global DRAM downturn — itself worsened by the technology-sector correction following the dot-com bust — carrying debt obligations that its operating cash flow could no longer service. In late 2001, the company entered a formal creditor workout, the Korean corporate restructuring mechanism administered by creditor banks rather than a bankruptcy court. The company was renamed [Hynix Semiconductor](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/company/profile.do). The moment marked the end of the Hyundai Group chapter and the beginning of a decade of creditor-controlled independence.

## Workout: Survival Under Creditor Control (2001–2012)

Korea Exchange Bank emerged as the lead creditor institution, guiding Hynix Semiconductor through successive rounds of debt restructuring, asset disposal, and operational rationalisation across the following decade. The workout era was neither swift nor comfortable. Hynix survived three distinct memory cycle downturns — the 2001–2002 bust, the 2007–2008 NAND-and-DRAM correction, and the 2008–2009 global financial crisis shock — each of which threatened to overwhelm a balance sheet still carrying workout-era legacy obligations.

The legal environment was equally hostile. Hynix Semiconductor faced significant intellectual property litigation from Rambus Inc., the memory interface licensing company that pursued DRAM producers aggressively through the 2000s. The Rambus litigation alleged that Hynix had engaged in anti-competitive conduct and infringed on Rambus's patented memory interface technologies; it consumed management attention and legal resources across multiple jurisdictions for years before being settled. The resolution removed a material litigation overhang that had complicated Hynix's credit profile and deterred potential acquirers.

Through the workout decade, Hynix Semiconductor's management focused on the core DRAM manufacturing competency, continuing to invest in process node migration even as the balance sheet constrained capital allocation. The company was not a technology laggard when the workout ended: its 30-nm and sub-30-nm DRAM node development kept pace with Samsung and Micron, and its NAND operations, though smaller than Samsung's, maintained commercial viability. What Hynix lacked was the strategic ownership and capital structure to invest at the scale required to compete for technology leadership rather than merely technology parity.

## The SK Group Acquisition: KRW 3.4 Trillion and a Strategic Wager (2012)

In November 2011, SK Group — the Korean conglomerate whose principal operations spanned telecommunications through SK Telecom, energy through SK Innovation, and chemicals through SK Materials — announced an agreement for an SK Telecom-led consortium to acquire the principal creditor stake in Hynix Semiconductor for approximately [KRW 3.4 trillion](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/press-releases). The transaction closed in February 2012, and the company was renamed SK Hynix.

The strategic rationale was layered. SK Telecom, then Korea's dominant mobile carrier, needed assured supply of mobile DRAM as smartphone penetration across Korea and Asia accelerated. At the group level, SK Chairman Choi Tae-won identified memory semiconductors as the category most likely to generate the durable free cash flows required to fund SK Group's broader industrial transformation over the following decade. The acquisition provided vertical integration into a component that touched every device across SK Telecom's customer base while positioning SK Group in the one sector of Korean industry where Samsung had built an advantage that felt permanent.

At KRW 3.4 trillion for a creditor-controlled workout survivor with a history of cyclical operating losses, the price was considered aggressive. Memory cycle timing was unfavourable: the announcement coincided with a severe DRAM downturn, and Hynix's balance sheet carried structural liabilities from the workout era. Critics within the Korean financial community questioned whether SK Group was acquiring a liability rather than an asset. The subsequent thirteen years rendered that criticism historically irrelevant — the 2012 acquisition stands as one of the most consequential conglomerate dealmaking decisions in modern Korean industrial history, measured by the EBITDA generation that followed.

## Building Scale in the SK Era: Fabs, Capex, and the NAND Diversification (2012–2021)

Under SK Group ownership, SK Hynix began a sustained programme of capital investment that the workout era had structurally prevented. The company invested in M15 in Cheongju, a large-scale fab oriented toward NAND Flash production that began operations in 2018, and followed with M16 in ~~Cheongju~~ ==Icheon==, a DRAM-focused facility whose progressive ramp extended into the 2020s. The M15 and M16 investments represented the most significant capacity expansion in the company's history, positioning SK Hynix to compete for NAND scale at a moment when the enterprise SSD market was expanding rapidly on the back of data centre buildout.

The NAND ambition found its fullest expression in October 2020, when SK Hynix announced the acquisition of Intel Corporation's NAND SSD business — including the Dalian, China fabrication facility — for a total consideration of approximately [USD 9 billion structured across two phases](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/press-releases). The first phase closed on 29 December 2021, transferring the NAND SSD business, the Dalian fab, and associated operational assets. A second phase covering the remaining wafer-fabrication intellectual property and operations ~~was expected to close in December 2025~~ ==closed on 27 March 2025 for approximately USD 1.9 billion, net of adjustments==.

The acquired business was organised into Solidigm Technology, a US-headquartered subsidiary based in ~~San Jose~~ ==Rancho Cordova==, California, ~~led by~~ ==initially led by== Rob Crooke, the former Intel senior vice president and general manager of Intel's Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group==, with David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh appointed co-CEOs of Solidigm in May 2023==. Solidigm gave SK Hynix a credible position in the enterprise NAND SSD market, a customer base spanning hyperscale data centre operators, and an Intel-derived technology lineage distinct from SK Hynix's internal NAND development — a strategic hedge against the commoditisation pressure bearing down on the broader NAND market.

## CEO Succession and the HBM Mandate (March 2024)

The management transition of March 2024 was orderly and deliberate. Park Jung-ho — who had arrived at SK Hynix as Vice Chairman and CEO in December 2021 following a career at SK Telecom that included the CEO role — had overseen the company's navigation of the severe 2023 memory downturn and the emergence of High Bandwidth Memory as the defining product of the AI infrastructure cycle. In March 2024, Park transitioned to Vice Chairman, ~~and [Kwak Noh-Jung assumed the CEO title](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/sustain/governance.do)~~ ==leaving [Kwak Noh-Jung — who had served as President & CEO since March 2022 — as the sole CEO of SK Hynix](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/sustain/governance.do)==.

Kwak's elevation carried a specific institutional logic. He had joined SK Hynix — then still Hynix Semiconductor — in 1994, had risen through semiconductor manufacturing operations over three decades, and had most recently served as President and Chief Production Officer. His doctoral training in ~~electrical engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology~~ ==materials engineering at Korea University== provided technical depth that complemented operational experience accumulated across the full cycle of SK Group ownership. Where Park had been the strategic architect of SK Group's HBM positioning, Kwak was the manufacturing operator who would execute it at volume scale during the most commercially consequential period in the company's history.

The transition reflected the broader SK Group governance convention of layered senior leadership: Park's continuing Vice Chairman role preserved strategic continuity while Kwak's operational authority over the principal SK Group profit centre was unambiguous.

## Thirteen Years: From Workout to Industry Pivot

The numerical testimony of the SK Group era requires little editorial elaboration.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Operating Profit/(Loss) (KRW T) |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 26.99 | — |
| 2020 | 31.90 | — |
| 2021 | 42.99 | — |
| 2022 | 44.62 | 6.81 |
| 2023 | 32.77 | (7.73) |
| 2024 | 66.19 | 23.47 |

*Source: [SK Hynix IR financial information](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information)*

The KRW 23.47 trillion operating profit posted in fiscal 2024 — a KRW 31 trillion year-on-year swing from the KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss of 2023 — was the steepest single-year recovery in the company's recorded history. The 2023 loss itself reflected the post-COVID inventory unwind combined with the pre-spending gap ahead of the AI infrastructure cycle; the 2024 recovery reflected SK Hynix's status as the principal scaled supplier of HBM to NVIDIA across the H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU generations, a supply position that commanded pricing premiums unavailable in the commodity DRAM spot market and reversed the historical assumption that Samsung's scale advantage in DRAM was structurally permanent.

SK Hynix entered SK Group in February 2012 as a workout survivor still clearing the liabilities of a government-engineered merger and a decade of creditor administration, its capital structure constrained, its legal docket still weighted with Rambus settlement obligations, its future ownership uncertain for the better part of a decade. It closed fiscal 2024 as the second-largest DRAM producer globally, the principal HBM supplier to the world's most consequential AI infrastructure customer, and the largest SK Group subsidiary by market capitalisation — a return on KRW 3.4 trillion that reshaped the competitive geography of the global memory industry.

chapters.title: DRAM, HBM, NAND, and Solidigm
chapters.body:
## A Three-Pillar Business Rebuilt Around One Strategic Bet

SK Hynix's revenue base entering 2024 rested on three structurally distinct product pillars: DRAM — the company's historic core and still its largest segment by revenue; NAND flash, substantially repositioned by the 2021 acquisition of Intel's storage business; and a smaller but growing CMOS image sensor operation. Within DRAM, a fourth dimension had emerged by 2023 that would redefine the company's financial identity: high bandwidth memory, or HBM, the stacked-DRAM architecture purpose-built for AI accelerator workloads. The interaction between these pillars — and the asymmetric margins HBM commanded over all of them — explained why SK Hynix's fiscal 2024 operating profit of KRW 23.47 trillion (~USD 17.8 billion) arrived as one of the most dramatic earnings recoveries in the memory industry's history.

## DRAM: Scale, Mix, and the Server Premium

SK Hynix held the number-two global position in DRAM by market share through the 2024 fiscal year, trailing only Samsung Electronics' Memory Business Division but ahead of Micron Technology. The DRAM segment itself was not monolithic. Server DRAM — principally DDR5 modules destined for hyperscaler and enterprise data-centre builds — represented the largest revenue contribution within the category, benefitting from both the structural cloud-capital-expenditure cycle and a generational node transition as hyperscalers refreshed Intel Sapphire Rapids and AMD Genoa platform inventory toward next-generation CPUs. Mobile DRAM, led by LPDDR5 and the higher-bandwidth LPDDR5X specification, formed the second-largest sub-segment, with Apple, Samsung Electronics' MX Division, Xiaomi, and Google Pixel among the principal procurement counterparties. Graphics DRAM — GDDR6, GDDR6X, and the emerging GDDR7 specification — addressed the broader discrete GPU market beyond the AI-accelerator HBM allocation, serving Nvidia's GeForce consumer line as well as AMD Radeon and embedded graphics customers.

| Sub-segment | Primary specification | Key customers |
|---|---|---|
| Server DRAM | DDR5 (up to 128GB RDIMM/LRDIMM) | AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta |
| Mobile DRAM | LPDDR5, LPDDR5X | Apple, Samsung MX, Xiaomi, Google |
| Graphics DRAM | GDDR6, GDDR6X, GDDR7 | Nvidia GeForce, AMD Radeon |
| HBM | HBM3, HBM3E, HBM4 (roadmap) | Nvidia H100/H200/Blackwell |
| Consumer/PC DRAM | DDR4, DDR5 UDIMM | OEM PC makers, retail channel |

The commodity DDR5 server segment and the mobile DRAM segment operated within the conventional memory-cycle pricing dynamic — boom-bust inventory replenishment cycles driven by end-demand and foundry-capacity additions. SK Hynix's manufacturing of these products ran principally through the Icheon complex in Gyeonggi Province, home to the M14 and M16 fabs, and the Cheongju facility where both DRAM and NAND wafer starts were managed against a shared capital base. An additional DRAM manufacturing operation in Wuxi, China provided capacity for the lower-end and mobile segments serving the China-market supply chain, though geopolitical dynamics around US export controls added a layer of strategic complexity to Wuxi's long-run utilisation.

## HBM: The Architecture of SK Hynix's Competitive Advantage

High bandwidth memory is, in structural terms, a premium DRAM product manufactured in a fundamentally different form factor. Where conventional DRAM ships as planar die on a PCB module, HBM is built by stacking multiple DRAM die vertically and interconnecting them through thousands of through-silicon vias — microscopic copper pillars punched through the silicon — before packaging the stack alongside the compute die in a single multi-chip module. The architecture collapses memory latency and explosively widens memory bandwidth at the cost of yield complexity, advanced packaging capability, and per-unit economics that bear no resemblance to commodity DRAM. Industry estimates through the 2024 fiscal year placed HBM gross margins at two to three times the gross margin on equivalent DRAM bit-count in commodity form.

SK Hynix's principal claim to strategic relevance in the AI infrastructure supply chain rested on one fact: it was the first memory manufacturer to qualify and ship HBM at scale to Nvidia, and it maintained that position through successive product generations. The HBM3 generation — the memory configuration deployed inside Nvidia's H100 and H200 accelerators, the dominant chips of the 2023–2024 data-centre AI build-out — was supplied principally by SK Hynix. When Nvidia's Blackwell architecture launched with the B100, B200, and GB200 products, SK Hynix again held the principal supplier position with HBM3E, the specification upgrade that extended per-stack bandwidth and capacity. Samsung Electronics, despite its larger overall DRAM market share, encountered yield and thermal qualification delays on its own HBM3E product that prevented meaningful Nvidia volume supply through most of 2024. Micron Technology entered the HBM3E market and captured some incremental share, but SK Hynix's cumulative lead in yield maturity and packaging kept it in the anchor supplier position.

The financial consequence was visible in the aggregate result. SK Hynix's fiscal 2024 revenue of KRW 66.19 trillion (~USD 50.2 billion) was more than double the KRW 32.77 trillion reported in fiscal 2023 — a year in which the company posted an operating loss of KRW 7.73 trillion, the steepest in its post-workout history. The KRW 31.2 trillion year-on-year operating-profit swing between 2023 and 2024 was not simply a commodity-DRAM cycle recovery; it was substantially the financial expression of HBM's margin premium multiplied through Nvidia's accelerating GPU production volume.

| Fiscal year | Revenue (KRW T) | Operating profit (KRW T) |
|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 42.99 | — |
| 2022 | 44.62 | 6.81 |
| 2023 | 32.77 | (7.73) |
| 2024 | 66.19 | 23.47 |

*Sources: [SK Hynix IR](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information); DART filings, KRX 000660*

~~Kwak Noh-jung, who assumed the chief executive role in March 2024 following Park Jung-ho's transition to Vice Chairman,~~ ==Kwak Noh-Jung, who has served as President & CEO of SK hynix since March 2022,== framed the competitive positioning in structural rather than cyclical terms. In remarks accompanying the company's earnings disclosures, he described SK Hynix's HBM lead as a function of accumulated manufacturing process knowledge — specifically the thermal interface materials, TSV drilling precision, and hybrid bonding capability developed over multiple product generations — rather than a fortuitous qualification accident. The implication was clear: the lead was defensible because it was embedded in process, not in product specification alone.

## HBM4 and the Rubin Roadmap

The competitive dynamics that generated SK Hynix's 2024 earnings would be renegotiated when Nvidia transitioned from the Blackwell generation to its successor, internally designated Rubin. HBM4 — the next-generation standard, specifying wider I/O, increased stack height, and substantially greater per-stack bandwidth — was the memory architecture Rubin required. SK Hynix ~~disclosed HBM4 sample shipments in 2024~~ ==announced shipment of the world's first 12-layer HBM4 samples to major customers on March 19, 2025== and publicly targeted a mass-production ramp in the second half of 2025. The qualification cycle at Nvidia for HBM4 represented the single most consequential near-term commercial event on SK Hynix's forward strategic calendar.

The competitive frame around HBM4 was different from HBM3E. Samsung Electronics, having suffered substantial reputational and commercial cost from its HBM3E qualification delays, entered the HBM4 development race with a stated intent to recover lost ground. Micron Technology, which had built credible HBM3E yield capability faster than Samsung, was positioned as a second viable HBM4 supplier. SK Hynix's principal risk was that HBM4's demand volume — driven by the scale of Nvidia's Rubin production build — would be large enough to require dual or triple sourcing, compressing SK Hynix's share below the near-monopoly position it held in HBM3 and early HBM3E supply windows.

## NAND Flash: Structural Position and the Solidigm Overlay

SK Hynix's NAND flash segment occupied a structurally different competitive position than its DRAM franchise. In NAND, SK Hynix ranked roughly third to fourth globally depending on bit-share measurement, behind Samsung Electronics and Kioxia, with Western Digital's NAND operations (being separated under the SanDisk brand through 2025) and Micron competitive in adjacent share bands. The commodity NAND market — serving mobile handsets, consumer SSDs, and the broader USB and embedded storage channel — generated lower average margins than server DRAM and far lower margins than HBM.

The 2021 acquisition of Intel's NAND and enterprise SSD business fundamentally repositioned SK Hynix's NAND franchise toward the enterprise and hyperscaler SSD segment. Announced in October 2020 for a total consideration of approximately USD 9.0 billion and structured as a two-phase close, the transaction transferred the NAND SSD business, the Dalian, China manufacturing facility, and key enterprise customer relationships in phase one (closed December 29, 2021), ~~with the remaining wafer-supply IP and operations scheduled for transfer by December 2025~~ ==with the second closing — covering the remaining NAND IP, R&D employees, and related assets — completed on March 27, 2025 for approximately USD 1.9 billion net of adjustments==.

## Solidigm: Enterprise SSDs and the Hyperscaler Relationship

The acquired business was rebranded as Solidigm Technology, headquartered in ~~San Jose~~ ==Rancho Cordova==, California. Rob Crooke — who had served as Senior Vice President and General Manager of Intel's Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group, the unit that built the QLC and Optane product families — led the subsidiary following the transaction close==, before Solidigm appointed David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh as co-CEOs in May 2023==. Solidigm's commercial identity centred on high-density QLC enterprise SSDs sold directly into hyperscaler procurement at AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta. The hyperscaler SSD market is structurally attractive: procurement volumes are large, contract relationships are durable, and the qualification cycles required to achieve design-in status create switching costs that differ from commodity NAND spot pricing.

Solidigm's manufacturing ran principally through the Dalian facility — a China-based operation that carried its own geopolitical exposure as US-China semiconductor trade tensions evolved through 2024 and 2025. The Dalian fab's status as the principal production base for an enterprise SSD business with major US hyperscaler customers created a structural tension that SK Hynix management acknowledged in investor communications as a risk factor requiring active management.

## CIS and Adjacent Products

SK Hynix's CMOS image sensor operation — legacy of earlier product diversification efforts — remained a smaller contributor to consolidated revenue. The CIS segment supplied image sensors to mobile handset OEMs and automotive camera applications, competing against Sony's dominant Semiconductor Solutions segment and Samsung's System LSI Division. The operation never achieved the scale necessary to rival either leader and occupied a subscale position within the company's broader portfolio, with capital allocation decisions in 2024 reflecting SK Hynix's concentration of investment in HBM and advanced DRAM packaging rather than CIS capacity expansion.

## Manufacturing Footprint as Strategic Asset

The physical geography of SK Hynix's production base reflected the layered accumulation of capacity decisions across three decades. The Icheon complex — the company's original Hyundai Electronics site — housed the M14 and M16 DRAM fabs and remained the principal node for advanced DRAM production, including the HBM wafer starts that fed the TSV packaging lines. Cheongju operated the M11 and M15 buildings, originally NAND-dedicated, with some DRAM capacity additions. Wuxi served the China-market DRAM supply chain. Dalian, under Solidigm, provided NAND wafer output for the enterprise SSD assembly lines.

The competitive moat embedded in this footprint was not primarily its scale — Samsung's aggregate fab capacity remained larger — but its concentration of advanced packaging capability at Icheon. Through-silicon-via drilling, hybrid bonding, and the thermal management processes required for eight-layer and twelve-layer HBM stacks demanded tooling investments and engineering process knowledge that could not be replicated quickly. It was this packaging depth, accumulated through SK Hynix's early commitment to HBM development beginning with HBM1 in the mid-2010s, that the company's 2024 earnings results made financially legible.

chapters.title: KRW 66T revenue and the KRW 31T operating-profit swing
chapters.body:
## The Return from the Abyss

When SK Hynix filed its full-year 2024 results, the headline figures arrived with the force of a decade's worth of deferred reckoning. Revenue reached KRW 66.19 trillion (~USD 50 billion) — more than double the KRW 32.77 trillion reported for fiscal 2023 — while operating profit came in at KRW 23.47 trillion, a swing of KRW 31.2 trillion from the KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss of the prior year. No comparable swing in either direction had appeared in SK Hynix's reporting history. The numbers were not merely cyclical recovery; they were structural revaluation, driven by a single product line that had, in the span of roughly thirty-six months, transformed the company's relationship with its most important customer.

That product was high-bandwidth memory. That customer was NVIDIA.

## Six Years of Revenue, One Picture

To understand what 2024 represented, it is necessary to read the revenue column in full. The following table traces SK Hynix's top line across the six fiscal years bracketing the AI memory transition:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | YoY Change |
|---|---|---|
| 2019 | 26.99 | — |
| 2020 | 31.90 | +18.2% |
| 2021 | 42.99 | +34.8% |
| 2022 | 44.62 | +3.8% |
| 2023 | 32.77 | −26.6% |
| 2024 | 66.19 | +102.0% |

*Source: [SK Hynix IR — Financial Information](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information)*

The 2021 print — KRW 42.99 trillion — reflected the post-COVID demand surge: server procurement, PC replacement cycles, and consumer electronics all expanding simultaneously. That year's performance was widely, and ultimately incorrectly, read as a new baseline. What followed was among the most severe corrections in the industry's modern history. By 2023, revenue had contracted KRW 11.85 trillion from the prior year and KRW 11.85 trillion from the 2021 peak, erasing more than three full fiscal years of growth in twelve months. The operating loss of KRW 7.73 trillion — the deepest single-year loss in more than a decade — captured what management would later describe as the combined pressure of a post-COVID inventory unwind and the gap period between the end of the prior spending cycle and the beginning of AI infrastructure build-out.

The 2024 line, KRW 66.19 trillion, is therefore not simply a large number. It is large against a very recent floor, and it exceeds the prior cycle peak by KRW 23.2 trillion — roughly the equivalent of adding another Samsung NAND franchise in revenue terms over a single fiscal year.

## Operating Leverage at the Cycle Turn

The operating profit column amplifies what the revenue column suggests. SK Hynix's cost structure — principally depreciation, wafer inputs, and process engineering — does not flex proportionately with revenue in either direction. This is the structural feature that makes memory semiconductor reporting so legible at cycle inflection points.

| Fiscal Year | Operating Profit (KRW T) |
|---|---|
| 2022 | 6.81 |
| 2023 | −7.73 |
| 2024 | 23.47 |

*Source: [SK Hynix IR — Financial Information](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information)*

The KRW 14.52 trillion collapse from 2022 to 2023 and the KRW 31.2 trillion recovery from 2023 to 2024 are expressions of the same underlying dynamic: a largely fixed cost base interacting with violently variable product pricing. What separates 2024 from a conventional cycle recovery is the degree to which SK Hynix's HBM franchise decoupled its DRAM gross margin from spot commodity pricing entirely.

In commodity DRAM — the DDR4 and DDR5 modules that flow through PC, server, and consumer channels — pricing is set by supply-demand dynamics at the module level and is visible in real time through broker indices. HBM is different. SK Hynix's HBM supply to NVIDIA across the HBM3 (H100, H200) and HBM3E (Blackwell B100, B200, GB200) generations was contracted on a supply-constrained basis, with pricing agreed bilaterally and not exposed to commodity spot markets. The premium commanded by HBM3E over an equivalent DRAM capacity in commodity DDR5 was substantial through 2024 — multiple analyst estimates placed HBM average selling prices at three to five times the per-gigabyte commodity equivalent, though SK Hynix does not disclose HBM ASPs independently.

Management commentary through 2024 earnings calls was consistent on the directional point. In disclosures accompanying the fourth-quarter 2024 results, SK Hynix indicated that HBM had come to represent a meaningful and growing share of total DRAM revenue and a disproportionate share of DRAM gross margin. The structural argument is straightforward: because HBM capacity is consumed inside NVIDIA's GPU systems before those systems are shipped, the demand signal is tied to NVIDIA's AI accelerator build schedule rather than to end-market server procurement cycles. This partially insulates SK Hynix's HBM revenue from the inventory overhang dynamics that drove the 2023 collapse in commodity segments.

## Capex and the Capacity Question

A recovery of this magnitude generates an immediate question about durability: to what extent was 2024's operating profit a function of supply discipline inherited from the 2023 downturn, and to what extent does it represent a sustainable margin structure?

The capex profile is central to this question. Memory semiconductor manufacturing requires continuous, large-scale investment in leading-edge process nodes. For SK Hynix in 2024, capex was running at elevated levels in two directions simultaneously: HBM capacity expansion, primarily at the Icheon campus in South Korea, and broader DRAM and NAND capacity maintenance and upgrade. The company had additionally committed to construction of a new ~~advanced DRAM fabrication facility~~ ==advanced packaging fabrication and R&D facility for AI products and HBM== in ==West Lafayette,== Indiana, United States — ==a roughly USD 3.87 billion project== announced ~~in 2023~~ with anticipated government support under the CHIPS and Science Act framework and targeting ~~production in the second half of the decade~~ ==mass production in the second half of 2028==.

SK Hynix does not break out capex by product line in its public quarterly disclosures, but the direction of management commentary through 2024 was unambiguous: HBM capacity expansion was the priority allocation, and broader capex discipline on commodity DRAM was being maintained deliberately as a mechanism to defend pricing. This is the standard memory-cycle management posture, observed at both Samsung and Micron as well, but SK Hynix's execution was credibility-tested by the severity of the 2023 loss: having sustained KRW 7.73 trillion in operating losses, the company had demonstrated the willingness to run at reduced utilisation rather than flood the commodity market.

The risk embedded in elevated HBM capex is one the market had largely priced by the time the 2024 results were published. If NVIDIA's AI accelerator shipment schedule were to slip — whether from export licensing constraints, hyperscaler budget discipline, or a competing architectural approach — HBM capacity would be stranded in a way that commodity DRAM capacity is not. HBM stacks are product-specific in their configuration; they are not fungible against commodity server DRAM without substantial yield loss. This is the other side of the premium pricing: SK Hynix's 2024 operating profit was partly a function of the fact that the company had made a large, irreversible bet on a single customer's demand trajectory and that bet paid off within the measurement window.

## The Debt Load from Solidigm

Against the operating profit recovery sits a balance sheet that carries the residual financing of the Intel NAND acquisition. The USD 9 billion total consideration for Solidigm Technology — structured across two phases, with Phase 1 closing December 29, 2021 and the ~~full transaction completing in late 2025~~ ==second closing occurring on March 27, 2025 for approximately USD 1.9 billion net of adjustments== — was the largest acquisition in SK Hynix's history and was financed substantially through debt. This was a deliberate strategic decision: SK Group wanted to scale into enterprise NAND and SSD markets without fully diluting the equity structure of the parent, and the financing was structured accordingly.

The debt load matters to the 2024 financial picture in two ways. First, interest expense is a direct charge against earnings, and with rates elevated through the 2022–2024 period, the servicing cost of the acquisition financing was not trivial against a backdrop of operating losses in 2023. Second, Solidigm's own operational performance through 2023 and into 2024 was under pressure from the same commodity NAND pricing collapse that affected all enterprise SSD suppliers. Solidigm's trajectory was not consolidated into SK Hynix's reported figures in the same line-item fashion as the core DRAM business, but SK Hynix's investor disclosures through the period acknowledged continued balance sheet reinforcement of the subsidiary.

The recovery of commodity NAND pricing through 2024, concurrent with the DRAM and HBM recovery, provided some natural hedge: the same inventory-unwind dynamics that had depressed pricing across both product categories into 2023 unwound across both in 2024. But Solidigm remained a balance-sheet complexity rather than a balance-sheet asset through the measurement window — a large, debt-financed bet on the enterprise SSD market that had not yet generated the returns that would retire the acquisition financing on its own cash flow.

## Cash Conversion and Capital Allocation

The operating profit recovery translated into strong operating cash flow generation in 2024. SK Hynix does not present a comprehensive US GAAP cash flow statement in its Korean IFRS filings in a format that is directly comparable to a US-listed issuer, but the directional picture from the quarterly disclosures is clear: after two years in which the company was drawing on credit facilities and managing working capital tightly against losses, 2024 restored the company to a position of meaningful free cash flow generation.

The principal uses of that cash flow were consistent with the capex priorities described above: HBM capacity, the Indiana facility land and preliminary construction, and continued Solidigm reinforcement. Dividends to shareholders were maintained through the downturn — a deliberate signal of financial stability to institutional investors — and were not materially increased in 2024, reflecting management's preference for retaining capital against the HBM capacity build.

The broader SK Group cross-financing dynamic is relevant context here. SK Hynix operates with significant operational autonomy as a KRX-listed entity with its own minority shareholders, but the SK Group parent — through SK Square — is both the controlling shareholder and the beneficiary of SK Hynix's capital allocation decisions. In periods of strong cash generation, the question of intra-group capital flows and the degree to which SK Hynix's balance sheet is managed in the context of broader SK Group treasury is one that minority investors have consistently raised. Through 2024, the principal capital allocation decision — elevated HBM capex at the expense of shareholder returns — was coherent with the standalone industrial logic of the company and did not appear to reflect intra-group considerations in any material way visible to outside investors.

## The Structural Read

The KRW 31 trillion operating-profit swing from 2023 to 2024 is a number that will appear in every institutional pitch book on the memory sector for a generation. The correct interpretive frame is not simply that SK Hynix recovered from a cyclical trough — every memory company did, to varying degrees. The correct frame is that SK Hynix recovered into a structurally superior position: it was the principal supplier of the product that drove the recovery, it was supply-constrained and contractually priced in that product, and its nearest competitor for that role had failed to achieve equivalent qualification status with the most important buyer in the market.

That competitive reality — Samsung's qualification gap on NVIDIA's HBM3E supply chain — is the single most consequential fact in the financial record. Without it, the 2024 numbers look like a strong cyclical recovery. With it, they look like the opening years of a structural franchise.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The simplest one-sentence description of SK Hynix's valuation predicament is also the most instructive: a company that produced KRW 23.47 trillion (approximately USD 17.3 billion) in operating profit in fiscal 2024 — the largest in its history ==at the time, since eclipsed by the FY2025 surge and a single Q1 2026 operating result of KRW 37.6 trillion==, representing a KRW 31 trillion year-on-year swing from the loss position recorded just twelve months earlier — ~~trades at a multiple that any growth-equity analyst would classify as negligible. This is not a valuation anomaly. It is the memory cycle discount, priced in through decades of institutional conditioning.~~ ==has seen its equity re-rate by roughly an order of magnitude through the HBM upcycle, closing 22 May 2026 near KRW 1.94 million per share. The traditional memory cycle discount has been substantially compressed; what remains contested is whether the new multiple regime is structurally earned.== The central question at the frozen snapshot date of May 2026 is whether the HBM franchise has ~~structurally invalidated that discount~~ ==structurally earned the re-rating already embedded in the price== — or whether history is about to rhyme.

## Sizing the Multiple

Precise market-cap arithmetic at the snapshot date requires a caveat: SK Hynix's KRX-listed shares (000660 KS) trade in Korean won, and the company's share count of approximately 728 million has been relatively stable through the recent capital cycle. Based on the ~~prevailing trading range of roughly KRW 155,000 to KRW 215,000 per share observed through the HBM upcycle~~ ==snapshot-date close of approximately KRW 1.94 million per share near 22 May 2026, with a recent trading band of roughly KRW 1.55 million to KRW 2.15 million==, the implied market capitalisation sits in the range of ~~KRW 113 trillion to KRW 157 trillion (approximately USD 82 billion to USD 114 billion at prevailing exchange rates)~~ ==KRW 1,130 trillion to KRW 1,570 trillion (approximately USD 820 billion to USD 1.14 trillion at prevailing exchange rates)==. For modelling purposes this analysis uses a midpoint of approximately ~~KRW 137 trillion (approximately USD 100 billion)~~ ==KRW 1,410 trillion (approximately USD 1.03 trillion)==, and all resulting multiples should be read as indicative within a band of roughly ±15%.

On that basis, the trailing price-to-earnings ratio on ~~fiscal 2024 net income — estimated at approximately KRW 19 trillion after net finance charges related to the Solidigm debt load and a normalised effective tax rate in the low-to-mid twenties (partially offset by deferred tax asset utilisation from the 2023 loss year) — produces a trailing P/E of roughly **7 to 9 times**~~ ==trailing-twelve-month net income through Q1 2026 — substantially elevated by the FY2025 HBM ramp and the record KRW 37.6 trillion Q1 2026 operating result — produces a trailing P/E in the area of **15 to 20 times**==. ~~Adding back estimated depreciation and amortisation of approximately KRW 11 to 12 trillion to reach a fiscal 2024 EBITDA of roughly KRW 35 trillion, and assuming net debt of approximately KRW 20 to 24 trillion (reflecting the multi-tranche Solidigm financing against a cash and equivalents position that has rebuilt sharply since the 2024 profit recovery), the trailing **EV/EBITDA lands at approximately 4.5 to 5 times**~~ ==On a trailing-twelve-month EBITDA basis updated for the FY2025 and Q1 2026 surge, and with the cash and equivalents position rebuilt sharply against the residual Solidigm debt load, the trailing **EV/EBITDA lands in the area of 10 to 13 times**==. Price-to-book, using ~~an estimated shareholders' equity of KRW 65 to 72 trillion accumulated through the HBM capex cycle~~ ==a shareholders' equity base that has compounded through the HBM capex cycle into the area of KRW 130 to 150 trillion==, comes to roughly ~~**1.9 to 2.1 times**~~ ==**9 to 11 times**==. Revenue ~~at KRW 66.19 trillion implies an **EV/Sales multiple of approximately 2.3 to 2.5 times**~~ ==on a trailing-twelve-month basis through Q1 2026 implies an **EV/Sales multiple of approximately 7 to 9 times**==.

## Where These Multiples Sit in Historical Context

The figures above ~~are neither anomalously cheap nor conspicuously rich by the standards of SK Hynix's own cycle history~~ ==sit well above the multiple band observed at any prior cyclical peak in SK Hynix's history==, but context matters. At the 2022 cyclical peak, before the post-COVID inventory correction erased KRW 7.73 trillion in operating profit across 2023, the stock traded at roughly 7 to 12 times trailing earnings and 4 to 7 times EV/EBITDA. Through the 2023 trough — when negative operating income made conventional earnings multiples meaningless — the stock held above KRW 90,000 per share on price-to-book support near 1.0 to 1.3 times, as investors marked the cycle bottom and front-ran the AI-driven recovery.

What is different in the current period is the composition of earnings. The 2022 peak was a commodity DRAM and NAND supercycle; the ~~2024 recovery~~ ==2024-2026 expansion== is a structurally margin-accretive HBM cycle, with HBM3E carrying an average selling price reported to be several multiples of equivalent-bandwidth commodity DRAM. The market ~~is beginning — tentatively — to re-rate on this basis, but it has not completed the repricing. The stock is trading at the high end of its own trailing range but has not broken decisively through the ceiling that historically marks cycle maturity~~ ==has aggressively re-rated on this basis, pricing the equity well above the multiple ceiling that historically marked cycle maturity==. The question is whether HBM structural pricing ~~lifts the ceiling or simply delays the usual descent~~ ==justifies the re-rating in perpetuity or whether the market will eventually re-impose the cycle discount==.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

| Company | Trailing P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | P/Book | HBM Position |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SK Hynix (000660 KS)** | ~~7–9×~~ ==~15–20×== | ~~4.5–5×~~ ==~10–13×== | ~~2.3–2.5×~~ ==~7–9×== | ~~2.0×~~ ==~9–11×== | Principal NVIDIA supplier (HBM3, HBM3E, HBM4 roadmap) |
| **Micron Technology (MU)** | ~10–14× | ~6–8× | ~3–4× | ~2.5–3.5× | Growing HBM3E; Blackwell qualification in progress |
| **Samsung Electronics (005930 KS)** | ~10–14× | ~7–9× | ~1.5–2× | ~1.2–1.5× | HBM3E qualification lag; conglomerate discount |
| **Kioxia ~~(6600 JP)~~ ==Holdings (285A TSE Prime)==** | ~8–12× | ~5–7× | ~1.5–2× | ~1.5–2× | NAND-only; no HBM exposure |
| **Western Digital / SanDisk (WDC)** | ~8–12× | ~5–7× | ~1.5–2× | ~2–3× | NAND-only; separation in progress |

The table encodes ~~the central irony of SK Hynix's valuation. The company holds the most commercially valuable position in the memory industry — principal scaled supplier of HBM3E to NVIDIA across the Blackwell generation — yet trades at a meaningful discount to Micron on every earnings-based multiple~~ ==SK Hynix's commercial leadership in HBM. The company holds the most valuable position in the memory industry — principal scaled supplier of HBM3E to NVIDIA across the Blackwell generation — and the market now awards it a meaningful premium to Micron on every earnings-based multiple==. ~~The Korea-to-US equity market discount is real, persistent, and partially structural: chaebol governance cross-shareholdings, thinner free float relative to market cap, and lower index inclusion weight all contribute. Micron's US listing, MSCI weighting, and accessibility to passive capital command a structural premium that is unlikely to compress absent an ADR uplisting or secondary listing — neither of which features on the current SK Hynix agenda.~~ ==The traditional Korea-to-US equity discount — chaebol governance cross-shareholdings, thinner free float relative to market cap, lower passive index inclusion weight — has been overpowered by the HBM revenue-mix story, with the market accepting that SK Hynix's HBM3E scale and HBM4 lead command a premium even net of the structural Korean discount. A US ADR uplisting or secondary listing would amplify the move further but does not feature on the current SK Hynix agenda.==

Samsung's position warrants separate treatment: the conglomerate structure means the semiconductor division is priced inside a sprawling vehicle that includes mobile handsets, displays, and consumer electronics. Sum-of-parts analysis consistently suggests the memory and foundry businesses alone would trade richer on a standalone basis. Samsung's HBM qualification delays with NVIDIA through 2024 and into 2025 are the single most important commercial datapoint enabling SK Hynix's premium multiple relative to Samsung — any Samsung requalification would be the most direct catalyst for multiple compression at SK Hynix.

## What the Current Price Implies: A DCF Frame

Working backwards from the midpoint market-cap estimate, the equity is discounting one of two terminal conditions. At a 10% cost of equity (appropriate for a Korean industrial with meaningful cycle risk), the current price is consistent with one of the following trajectories: a sustained earnings stream of approximately ~~KRW 15 to 18 trillion~~ ==KRW 110 to 140 trillion== per year in perpetuity with modest terminal growth; or a near-term earnings stream of ~~KRW 20 to 25 trillion~~ ==KRW 150 to 200 trillion== declining to a cycle-normalised level of ~~KRW 8 to 10 trillion~~ ==KRW 60 to 80 trillion== by the late 2020s, as HBM pricing mean-reverts. The former implies the market has accepted the structural HBM margin thesis. The latter implies classic cycle discounting applied to peak earnings. The stock price as of the snapshot date appears to be pricing ~~something between the two — an acknowledgement that HBM matters, but hedged heavily by institutional memory of how aggressively DRAM pricing has corrected in every prior supercycle~~ ==closer to the structural-acceptance trajectory than to the cycle-discounting one, with institutional memory of DRAM mean reversion substantially overridden by HBM's demonstrated pricing power across the FY2024-Q1 2026 sequence==.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bear case — KRW ~~90,000 to 120,000~~ ==900,000 to 1,200,000== per share.** Samsung Electronics qualifies HBM3E at scale with NVIDIA during 2025, the duopoly dynamic that defined the HBM3E cycle breaks down, and ASP pressure materialises. Concurrently, AI infrastructure spending moderates — either through hyperscaler capex discipline or NVIDIA's own supply-chain diversification — and total HBM volumes disappoint. SK Hynix's operating profit contracts toward KRW ~~10 to 13~~ ==45 to 60== trillion. At ~~4 to 5~~ ==5 to 6== times EV/EBITDA on a normalised EBITDA base of KRW ~~22 to 25~~ ==85 to 100== trillion, and adjusting for net debt, the equity component compresses to the KRW ~~90,000 to 120,000~~ ==900,000 to 1,200,000== range. This scenario assigns a multiple broadly consistent with commodity DRAM peak-cycle pricing — a conscious refusal to award any HBM structural premium.

**Base case — KRW ~~155,000 to 200,000~~ ==1,550,000 to 2,000,000== per share.** The HBM3E ramp sustains through the full Blackwell cycle, HBM4 for Rubin begins contributing to revenue by late 2026, and Samsung's qualification remains at least two to three quarters behind. Operating profit ~~moderates toward KRW 18 to 21 trillion~~ ==moderates toward KRW 90 to 120 trillion== as some ASP compression is offset by volume growth. The market ~~partially re-rates — not to software multiples, but to 5.5 to 6.5~~ ==holds the current re-rating, not at software multiples but at 9 to 11== times EV/EBITDA, acknowledging that HBM introduces a durable margin floor absent in prior cycles. The resulting equity value is in the KRW ~~155,000 to 200,000~~ ==1,550,000 to 2,000,000== range, approximating the current trading midpoint. This scenario essentially validates the current price.

**Bull case — KRW ~~250,000 to 320,000~~ ==2,500,000 to 3,200,000== per share.** SK Hynix extends its HBM4 qualification lead well into 2027, cementing the role of sole or overwhelmingly dominant HBM supplier to NVIDIA's Rubin and successor platforms. HBM4 ASPs expand relative to HBM3E given the significantly higher compute density of the AI-accelerator addressable market. Operating profit grows toward KRW ~~26 to 32~~ ==160 to 200== trillion, and the investment community — informed by several consecutive quarters of proof that HBM pricing does not mean-revert like commodity DRAM — ~~re-rates the stock to 7 to 9~~ ==expands the multiple further to 13 to 15== times EV/EBITDA. A simultaneous narrowing of the Korea-to-US multiple gap (or a US listing event, which is speculative) amplifies the move. The resulting equity value implies a market capitalisation approaching or exceeding USD ~~200 billion~~ ==1.6 trillion== — a re-rating that would place SK Hynix among the most valuable pure-play semiconductor businesses globally.

## The Gap Between Consensus and This Dossier's Read

The sell-side consensus at the snapshot date appears to be comfortably parked in the base case, with price targets clustering in the KRW ~~160,000 to 210,000~~ ==1,600,000 to 2,100,000== range and 12-month forward P/E estimates in the ~~high single digits~~ ==mid-teens==. What consensus appears to underweight is the asymmetry of the HBM qualification position: the lead SK Hynix holds over Samsung is not merely a procurement calendar advantage but reflects a years-long investment in chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging, thermal management, and silicon integrity testing that Samsung has found structurally difficult to replicate on NVIDIA's timeline. Each quarter that Samsung's qualification fails to close is a quarter in which SK Hynix's pricing power is less contested than conventional cycle analysis would predict.

This dossier reads the bull case probability at approximately 25 to 30 percent — meaningfully above implied options market pricing, which tends to anchor to historical memory cycle volatility rather than the altered competitive dynamics that HBM structural supply constraints have introduced. The base case remains the modal outcome, but the skew is positive: the downside is bounded by a capital structure that has substantially repaired since the Solidigm debt load peak, while the upside from a multi-year HBM technology lead compounding into HBM4 and HBM4E is not yet fully reflected in consensus price targets. The memory cycle discount ~~may not be retired, but it has been meaningfully recalibrated~~ ==has been substantially retired, and the surviving valuation debate is whether the new multiple regime is structurally earned rather than whether the historical discount still applies==.

chapters.title: From the 2023 trough to the 2024 record
chapters.body:
## A Decade's Worst Downturn

By the fourth quarter of 2022, the inflection was already legible in SK Hynix's order pipeline. Hyperscaler customers that had accumulated server DRAM inventory through the supply-constrained years of 2020 and 2021 began cutting procurement sharply as the data-centre expansion that defined the post-pandemic period moderated. Mobile DRAM customers — Apple for the iPhone 14 cycle, Samsung's handset division, and the major Chinese Android manufacturers — trimmed LPDDR5 commitments as consumer device demand compressed. SK Hynix closed fiscal 2022 with KRW 6.81 trillion in operating profit, a result that was already deteriorating through the second half of the year as the inventory overhang made itself felt across both DRAM and NAND product lines.

The reckoning arrived in earnest in the first quarter of 2023, when the company recorded its first quarterly operating loss. The losses deepened through the second and third quarters as average selling prices fell faster than the company's cost-reduction programmes could compensate. DRAM spot prices, particularly commodity DDR5 server configurations, reached multi-year lows through the middle of the year. NAND pricing fell in parallel. Gross margins inverted. Operating expenses in semiconductor manufacturing, substantially fixed in nature, could not be compressed at the pace of the revenue collapse.

By the close of fiscal 2023, SK Hynix had recorded a full-year operating loss of KRW 7.73 trillion (approximately USD 5.7 billion) on revenue of KRW 32.77 trillion — a revenue contraction of roughly 27 percent from the KRW 44.62 trillion of 2022, and a cumulative operating profit swing of nearly KRW 14.5 trillion in a single year. It was the steepest downturn in the company's history, eclipsing the damage of the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the 2015–2016 NAND oversupply episode.

## Navigating the Trough

Under CEO ~~Park Jung-ho~~ ==Kwak Noh-Jung==, the company's response combined production discipline with selective investment. SK Hynix materially reduced capital expenditure commitments for commodity DRAM and NAND through 2023 while ring-fencing development spending in high-bandwidth memory. The strategic logic was clear from the company's public communications: SK Hynix held a structural technology lead in HBM, and competing for commodity volume at destructive pricing would erode the financial foundation needed to sustain that advantage. ~~Park~~ ==Kwak== told investors through the cycle that the company would absorb the downturn rather than sacrifice long-term positioning for near-term revenue, framing the loss year as the cost of a deliberate triage.

The aggregate annual loss figure obscures a critical fourth-quarter inflection. SK Hynix's [press releases](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/press-releases) confirm that NVIDIA's H100 training accelerator, which drew on SK Hynix's HBM3 production as the principal qualified supplier, began contributing meaningfully to revenue mix in the fourth quarter of 2023. NVIDIA had qualified SK Hynix as the primary HBM3 source for the H100 and H200 — the GPUs anchoring the first major wave of large language model infrastructure buildout — and the ramp accelerated through the second half of the year. Commodity DRAM contract prices also began recovering in the fourth quarter, modestly, but the directional shift was sufficient for investors to begin pricing the recovery. The sequential improvement from the third to the fourth quarter of 2023 marked the effective floor of the cycle.

## The HBM3 Premium and the 2024 Return to Profit

SK Hynix reported its first quarterly operating profit of the recovery cycle in the first quarter of 2024~~, arriving precisely as the March 2024 CEO transition from Park Jung-ho to Kwak Noh-Jung was completed~~. Kwak — ~~who holds a PhD in electrical engineering from KAIST and had spent thirty years in SK Hynix's semiconductor manufacturing operations, most recently as President and Chief Production Officer — assumed the CEO role as the financial trajectory was already reversing~~ ==who holds a Ph.D. in Materials Engineering from Korea University and had spent thirty years in SK Hynix's semiconductor manufacturing operations, including a stint as President and Chief Production Officer before assuming the CEO role in March 2022 — watched the financial trajectory reverse in his third year at the helm==. His ~~early~~ public communications were oriented not toward defending against losses but toward sustaining the qualification advantage that was driving the recovery.

The first-quarter profit print reflected two converging forces. HBM3 revenue on the H100 and H200 platforms had reached meaningful scale, and the premium that HBM3 commanded over commodity DRAM per-bit — several multiples higher on a per-gigabyte basis — was reshaping the company's revenue mix in ways that aggregate DRAM pricing indices did not capture. Simultaneously, commodity server DRAM and mobile DRAM pricing completed their recovery from trough levels as hyperscaler inventory clearance finished and renewed AI server procurement began absorbing fresh DRAM alongside HBM.

Operating profit accelerated quarter by quarter through 2024. The second-half results were the strongest in the company's history. SK Hynix had secured the principal qualified supplier position for HBM3E on NVIDIA's Blackwell generation — comprising the B100, B200, and GB200 — ahead of Samsung Electronics, whose own HBM3E qualification on Blackwell was delayed through much of 2024. Each Blackwell GPU ships with a stack of HBM3E; NVIDIA's GPU shipment volumes in 2024 translated directly into SK Hynix supply volumes at premium pricing.

Kwak, in communications with investors ~~through his first year as CEO~~ ==through 2024==, characterised the HBM franchise not as an opportunistic windfall but as the return on a technology investment programme that predated the AI cycle's emergence as a commercial reality. The qualification primacy on Blackwell, he indicated, was earned through years of process development — including the advanced thermal interface and through-silicon-via architecture required for HBM3E — rather than a function of cycle timing.

## The Record Year

The full-year 2024 [results](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information) confirmed what the quarterly progression had signalled. Revenue reached KRW 66.19 trillion (approximately USD 49 billion), more than doubling the KRW 32.77 trillion of 2023. Operating profit came in at KRW 23.47 trillion (approximately USD 17.4 billion).

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Op. Profit / (Loss) (KRW T) | Revenue YoY |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 42.99 | — | — |
| 2022 | 44.62 | +6.81 | +3.8% |
| 2023 | 32.77 | −7.73 | −26.6% |
| 2024 | 66.19 | +23.47 | +102.0% |

*Source: [SK Hynix Investor Relations](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information)*

The year-on-year operating profit swing — from a KRW 7.73 trillion loss to a KRW 23.47 trillion profit — was a KRW 31.2 trillion movement, by a considerable margin the largest single-year earnings recovery in SK Hynix's history. The full-year operating margin of approximately 35.5 percent was a level the company had not approached in any prior fiscal year.

The 2024 result was not merely a cyclical normalisation. The operating margin profile reflected the structural premium that HBM commands — a premium that, unlike commodity DRAM, is anchored in the qualification relationship with a concentrated customer base where switching costs are high. Samsung's slower qualification path on Blackwell left SK Hynix without a volume competitor on NVIDIA's most commercially important GPU family through most of the year. Micron Technology also built HBM3E capability but entered the supply chain at smaller scale.

## 2025: HBM4 and the Competitive Realignment

The progression into 2025 added a further dimension to the structural debate. HBM4 — the next-generation architecture targeting NVIDIA's Rubin platform and analogous successors — entered active qualification work. SK Hynix publicly positioned itself to extend the supply relationship to the Rubin generation, and Kwak's communications through 2025 framed HBM4 readiness as the company's primary strategic execution priority.

The competitive backdrop intensified. Samsung, acutely aware of the commercial cost of its HBM3E qualification lag, committed substantial resources to closing the gap, and both Samsung and Micron made measurable HBM3E share gains through the first half of 2025. The qualification duopoly that SK Hynix had briefly held on Blackwell did not persist indefinitely. But SK Hynix entered 2025 as the dominant supplier in a market that was still volume-constrained by NVIDIA's own GPU production ramp — incremental share gains by competitors were taken against an expanding total addressable volume rather than from a fixed pool.

The company's equity reflected the structural reassessment. SK Hynix ranked among the best-performing large-cap names on the Korea Exchange in 2024 and through 2025, as investors re-rated the stock upward on evidence that the HBM premium represented a multi-year structural shift in the memory industry's earnings profile. For an industry that had historically been valued at steep discounts through the cycle — on the assumption that semiconductor memory margins were inherently mean-reverting — the HBM earnings persistence challenged conventional frameworks for how the memory business should be priced.

The fiscal arc from 2023 to 2024 is ultimately the account of a bet sustained through an unfashionable era. The investment in HBM capability that produced SK Hynix's qualification primacy on H100, H200, and Blackwell was made in years when AI infrastructure demand existed as a forecast rather than a revenue line. The KRW 7.73 trillion loss of 2023 was the cost of holding that position through the trough. The KRW 23.47 trillion profit of 2024 was the validation.

chapters.title: Kwak, Park, Crooke, and the SK Group governance frame
chapters.body:
## The March 2024 Handoff

When SK Hynix announced in March 2024 that ~~Kwak Noh-Jung would assume the chief executive role from Park Jung-ho~~ ==Park Jung-ho would step back from his co-CEO role, leaving Kwak Noh-Jung — President & CEO since March 2022 — as sole chief executive==, the transition carried a logic specific to the moment. Park had spent two and a half years steering the company through the 2023 downturn — the deepest memory-industry correction in a generation — and into the earliest stages of an HBM-led recovery. The handoff preserved what Park had built while ~~installing an operator~~ ==consolidating authority in an operator== whose entire professional life had unfolded inside SK Hynix's fabrication halls. Park moved to Vice Chairman, ~~retaining a board seat and broader strategic oversight~~ ==stepping off the SK Hynix board while retaining a broader strategic-oversight remit within the SK Group orbit==. The continuity was deliberate: the company was about to deliver KRW 23 trillion in operating profit in 2024, and no one in management wanted to introduce discontinuity at an inflection point.

The structure that emerged — a semiconductor-native CEO supported by a strategist Vice Chairman drawn from the broader SK Group orbit — mirrored the layered senior leadership architecture visible elsewhere in Korean chaebol conglomerates, where succession rarely means clean severance.

## Kwak Noh-Jung: Thirty Years Inside the Machine

Kwak joined what was then Hyundai Electronics in 1994, four years before the Asian financial crisis forced the company into the creditor workout that would eventually produce the modern SK Hynix. He did not leave. Across three decades — through the 2001 Hynix Semiconductor rebranding, the 2012 SK Group acquisition, and the successive memory cycles that followed — Kwak accumulated seniority inside the company's manufacturing operations, rising eventually to President and Chief Production Officer before the board elevated him to ==co-==chief executive ==in March 2022==.

His academic grounding — a doctorate in ~~electrical engineering from KAIST, Korea's foremost science and technology research university~~ ==Materials Engineering from Korea University== — is directly legible in his operational priorities. ~~KAIST PhDs who~~ ==Materials-engineering doctorates who== enter semiconductor manufacturing tend to embed themselves in process yield and node transition problems rather than in corporate finance or marketing, and Kwak's three-decade arc followed that pattern. As Chief Production Officer he oversaw the fabrication infrastructure that produced SK Hynix's decisive move into high-bandwidth memory, including the Icheon and Cheongju wafer fabs where HBM stacking lines were progressively scaled. By the time he ~~took the CEO title~~ ==assumed sole stewardship in March 2024==, his institutional knowledge of SK Hynix's manufacturing bottlenecks, process genealogy, and supplier dependencies was effectively unmatched inside the company.

The strategic mandate Kwak ~~inherited~~ ==assumed as sole CEO== in March 2024 was one of execution continuity: maintain the HBM supply relationship with NVIDIA across HBM3 and the ramp of HBM3E, manage the capital expenditure cycle responsibly given the scale of the 2024 recovery, and ensure that the development pipeline for next-generation HBM architectures remained ahead of Samsung. The CEO who had spent his entire career understanding exactly how wafers move through SK Hynix's fab network was, by that measure, precisely calibrated for the task.

## Park Jung-ho: The Telecom Executive Who Rebuilt a Memory Company

Park Jung-ho arrived at SK Hynix in December 2021 as Vice Chairman and CEO, bringing a background that was conspicuously different from the semiconductor-manufacturing tradition. He had previously served as chief executive of SK Telecom, the dominant South Korean mobile carrier and a sister operating company within the SK Group conglomerate. That background was not incidental. Park joined at a moment when memory had become infrastructure — when the question of how NAND and DRAM sat within hyperscaler and data-centre procurement chains was as important as the question of how to manufacture them.

Park's tenure covered one of the most volatile stretches in SK Hynix's modern history. The company entered 2022 with post-pandemic demand expectations that cratered through the year; by 2023 it was booking operating losses as the inventory glut across DRAM and NAND compressed prices across the industry. His decision to curtail capital expenditure during the downturn — resisting the temptation to maintain output volume in a falling-price environment — helped preserve the balance sheet ahead of the AI-driven HBM surge that materialised in the second half of 2023 and accelerated through 2024. [SK Hynix IR press releases, skhynix.com/eng/ir] The strategic relationship with NVIDIA, which anchored SK Hynix as the dominant supplier of HBM3 for the H100 GPU generation, was substantially structured during the Park era.

When Park moved to Vice Chairman in March 2024, ~~he retained a board seat as an executive director.~~ ==he stepped off the SK Hynix board, with the subsequent director slate reflecting his departure.== The arrangement preserved his relationships with the SK Group holding structure and with the principal external stakeholders — hyperscaler procurement executives, Korean government officials overseeing semiconductor industrial policy, and the broader financial community that had watched him navigate the 2023 trough — while allowing Kwak to assume operational authority.

## The Operating Layer

Below Kwak and Park, a four-person operating team divided the principal functional responsibilities.

Justin Kim — known in Korean as Kim Joohyun — carried the President of Business title, with accountability spanning customer engagement, marketing, and commercial operations across SK Hynix's full product portfolio. In practical terms, that placed him at the centre of the NVIDIA HBM supply relationship, the single most commercially consequential customer engagement in the semiconductor industry through the 2023–2026 AI infrastructure cycle. Managing that relationship required not just product and yield visibility but the kind of sustained executive-level access that Park had cultivated and that Justin Kim was responsible for perpetuating.

Kim Woo-hyun held the CFO role, overseeing financial planning, treasury, investor relations, and the corporate-finance infrastructure that had processed one of the more complex acquisition financing sequences in recent Korean industrial history. The 2021 agreement to acquire Intel's NAND business for approximately $9 billion — completed in stages, with the final tranche closing in 2025 — required structured financing arrangements that sat on SK Hynix's balance sheet through a period of sharply negative free cash flow in 2023 before the HBM recovery rebuilt earnings capacity. [SK Hynix IR, skhynix.com/eng/ir; SEC EDGAR CIK 0001687247] Kim Woo-hyun's investor-relations posture through that period — communicating the company's capital-allocation discipline to an investor base that had seen Korean memory companies mismanage downturns before — was central to the confidence the company maintained in credit markets.

Cha Jin-suk, as President of Development, bore direct responsibility for the technology pipeline that had made SK Hynix's HBM lead structurally durable rather than transient. The development function's output through the 2022–2025 period included the successive HBM3 and HBM3E generations delivered to NVIDIA, plus the DRAM and NAND roadmaps that kept the broader product portfolio competitive. The competitive gap between SK Hynix and Samsung in HBM yield, stack reliability, and thermal performance — visible in NVIDIA's public procurement posture — reflected the accumulated decisions made within Cha's organisation.

Lee Sang-rak, as President of Manufacturing and Technology, was the functional counterpart to the development layer: where Cha's organisation produced the process specifications, Lee's organisation translated them into production-scale execution across the Icheon M16 facility and the broader fab network. The manufacturing function's performance on HBM yield at scale was the proximate determinant of how much revenue the development organisation's roadmap success could actually deliver.

## Rob Crooke and the Solidigm Bridge

Rob Crooke occupied a structurally distinct position within the SK Hynix executive ecosystem ==during Solidigm's first eighteen months as a subsidiary==. A former Intel senior vice president and general manager of the Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group, Crooke was the executive who had managed the Intel NAND business through the years immediately preceding the SK Hynix acquisition agreement.
