When SK Hynix completed the first phase of the transaction in late 2021, Crooke became ~~President~~ ==CEO== of Solidigm — the rebranded entity, headquartered in ~~San Jose~~ ==Rancho Cordova, California==, that carried forward Intel's enterprise SSD franchise as a US-based SK Hynix subsidiary.

The Solidigm role gave SK Hynix something the Icheon-headquartered parent organisation had not previously possessed at scale: a US-rooted executive with deep relationships across hyperscaler and enterprise storage procurement, built through years of selling into Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and the major enterprise OEMs under the Intel brand. Those relationships — Intel's Optane and QLC NAND customer base — did not vanish at the point of acquisition, and Crooke's continuity ==through the integration's launch phase== provided the commercial anchor that retained them within the SK Hynix consolidated revenue line. ==By May 2023, Solidigm had appointed David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh as co-CEOs, with Crooke stepping back from day-to-day leadership; the subsidiary's commercial relationships and integration trajectory have carried forward under the new leadership team.== The Solidigm subsidiary represented SK Hynix's most direct exposure to the US enterprise storage market and the most tangible integration challenge of the multi-phase acquisition.

## The SK Group Governance Frame

Above the operating management layer sat the board of directors and, through it, the broader SK Group governance architecture.

~~Choi Tae-won, Chairman of SK Group, served as chairman of the SK Hynix board — the principal shareholder-level governance anchor within a conglomerate structure that had SK Inc., SK Telecom, and SK Hynix as its three principal operating pillars.~~ ==Choi Tae-won, Chairman of SK Group, sat at the apex of a conglomerate structure whose principal operating pillars included SK Inc., SK Square, SK Telecom, and SK Hynix, but did not himself hold a seat on the SK Hynix board; board chairmanship was held by independent director Ko Seung-Beom.== By 2024, SK Hynix had become the SK Group's largest subsidiary by market capitalisation on the strength of its HBM recovery, a reversal of the historical weighting that had treated SK Telecom as the conglomerate's flagship asset. That shift in proportional significance elevated the SK Hynix board to a degree of strategic centrality within the SK Group holding structure that it had not previously held.

The board paired ~~the three executive directors — Choi, Kwak, and Park — with five independent directors~~ ==inside directors Kwak Noh-Jung and Cha Seon-Yong with other non-executive directors Jang Yong-Ho and Kim Jung-Kyu and a slate of independent directors chaired by Ko Seung-Beom== whose collective expertise addressed the principal governance demands of a company operating at the intersection of semiconductor manufacturing, AI infrastructure supply, and international capital markets.

~~Kim Yang-bin brought corporate governance and business oversight experience to the board's committee work. Yoon Hye-li, with a legal background, anchored the compliance and audit committee responsibilities that a company with cross-border operations, DART disclosure obligations in Korea, and SEC-equivalent filings through its 20-F equivalent required. Cho Hyun-jae, drawing on academic and governance experience, contributed to the risk-management and compensation committee frameworks. Han Aerin's finance background provided independent oversight of the capital allocation and remuneration decisions that a company deploying tens of trillions of won in capital expenditure across a cycle required. Ha Young-gu, with technology-industry experience, brought the sector-specific perspective necessary to assess the company's R&D investment decisions and technology roadmap commitments independently of management advocacy.~~ ==Ko Seung-Beom's chairmanship anchored the independent slate, whose remit covered the compliance and audit committee responsibilities a company with cross-border operations, DART disclosure obligations in Korea, and SEC-equivalent filings through its 20-F equivalent required; the risk-management and compensation committee frameworks; independent oversight of the capital allocation and remuneration decisions that a company deploying tens of trillions of won in capital expenditure across a cycle required; and the sector-specific perspective necessary to assess R&D investment decisions and technology roadmap commitments independently of management advocacy.==

The Korean public-company governance framework within which this board operated — mandating audit committee independence, disclosure requirements via DART, and shareholder protections calibrated to the specific features of chaebol-controlled public companies — shaped the board's formal authority over executive appointments, remuneration, and major capital allocation decisions. The cross-shareholding structure that gave SK Group its controlling position in SK Hynix was a feature of the broader Korean conglomerate model rather than specific to SK Hynix: ~~SK Inc. held its SK Hynix stake~~ ==SK Square held the direct major-shareholder stake in SK Hynix — 146,118,388 shares, or 20.5% of issued capital —== as part of the layered ownership chain that Choi Tae-won controlled at the apex. [Korea Financial Services Commission DART filings]

The governance arrangement that resulted — a chaebol-controlled company with a technically sophisticated CEO, a strategically experienced Vice Chairman, a professional operating team, and an independent board with functional expertise across law, finance, technology, and governance — reflected the institutional maturation that the SK Group had pursued since the 2012 acquisition converted a distressed creditor workout into one of the most valuable semiconductor businesses on Earth.

chapters.title: NVIDIA, hyperscalers, mobile OEMs, and the equipment supply chain
chapters.body:
## The NVIDIA Relationship: A Franchise Built on HBM3

No single commercial relationship transformed SK Hynix's financial trajectory more decisively than its position as the principal scaled supplier of high-bandwidth memory to NVIDIA. When NVIDIA began ramping H100 production in earnest through 2023 and into 2024, SK Hynix's HBM3 stacks were the memory substrate that made the accelerator viable at hyperscaler scale. The dependency was mutual and structural: NVIDIA's data-centre GPU roadmap required a memory partner capable of delivering HBM at volume with the thermal and bandwidth tolerances the H100 architecture demanded, and SK Hynix had accumulated the manufacturing depth — particularly in through-silicon via packaging — that Samsung, despite its broader scale in DRAM, could not replicate at the qualification milestones NVIDIA required.

The HBM3 supply relationship extended through the H200 generation, which used a higher-capacity HBM3 stack configuration and reached hyperscaler deployments through the second half of 2024. When NVIDIA transitioned to the Blackwell architecture — the B100, B200, and GB200 accelerators — the memory specification moved to HBM3E, and SK Hynix again held the principal supplier position. The KRW 23.47 trillion operating profit SK Hynix reported for fiscal 2024, a swing of approximately KRW 31 trillion from the KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss of 2023, was driven in substantial part by the HBM premium embedded in these supply agreements. The average selling price differential between HBM3E and a comparable DRAM capacity in conventional DDR5 configuration was, by the time of the 2024 annual results, estimated by industry analysts to be a multiple of four to six times on a per-gigabyte basis — a pricing premium that flowed directly through to SK Hynix's gross margin.

Forward positioning for the next generation was underway by the frozen snapshot date. HBM4, targeting NVIDIA's Rubin GPU architecture, requires a logic base die manufactured on an advanced process node — a structural departure from prior HBM generations, which used SK Hynix's own memory process for the base die. The company disclosed in its 2024 earnings materials and subsequent investor communications that it was pursuing qualification work on HBM4 with customer timelines aligned to the Rubin ramp. This development introduced a foundry dimension to the HBM supply chain that had not previously existed, with TSMC's advanced logic process expected to serve as the base die manufacturer for leading suppliers.

## Broader AI Accelerator Customers

NVIDIA was the dominant customer by revenue, but SK Hynix's HBM and advanced DRAM exposure extended across the broader AI accelerator ecosystem. AMD's MI300X accelerator, which reached volume deployment at Microsoft Azure and other hyperscalers through 2024, relied on HBM3. The MI325X and early MI350 configurations used HBM3E. SK Hynix was among the qualified suppliers across the AMD accelerator programme, alongside Micron, which had also qualified HBM3E by mid-2024.

The custom silicon programmes at the large hyperscalers created a more opaque but structurally significant second layer of HBM demand. AWS Trainium and Inferentia accelerators, Google's Tensor Processing Units, and Microsoft's Maia silicon all incorporated HBM or advanced DRAM at the memory subsystem level. Supply relationships for custom silicon of this kind are rarely disclosed at the component-supplier level by either party, and SK Hynix's IR materials did not specify volume shares for individual hyperscaler custom programmes. What is clear from the aggregate trajectory — fiscal 2024 HBM revenue that the company indicated had grown to a substantial proportion of total DRAM revenue — is that NVIDIA represented the largest single vector but not the only one.

## Server DRAM: DDR5 at the Hyperscaler Infrastructure Layer

Beneath the HBM tier sits the broader server DRAM layer, where DDR5 had become the dominant specification at hyperscaler new-server deployments by 2024. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle represent the principal server DRAM buyers at the hyperscaler tier. SK Hynix competed for this volume alongside Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology — the three-supplier duopoly that characterises qualified server DRAM supply at every major cloud provider.

DDR5 qualification cycles at hyperscalers are multi-quarter processes that require suppliers to pass thermal, reliability, and compatibility testing against the specific server platforms the customer deploys. SK Hynix held qualification status across the principal hyperscaler server programmes through 2024. The server DRAM market does not carry the pricing premium of HBM — it is a more competitive, more commoditised segment — but it provides volume throughput that keeps DRAM fabs at utilisation and contributes to the cost-absorption economics that underpin HBM manufacturing capacity investment.

## Mobile DRAM: Apple and the Premium OEM Channel

Apple has historically been the most demanding and most strategically significant mobile DRAM customer in the industry. The qualification cycle for LPDDR5 supply to the iPhone platform is among the most rigorous in consumer electronics: Apple's process involves extended reliability testing, thermal cycle validation, and yield-at-package-level verification before a supplier achieves and holds volume allocation. SK Hynix held qualified status as an LPDDR5 supplier to Apple across the iPhone 15 and iPhone 16 product cycles, a position it shared with Samsung Semiconductor, which also supplied Apple mobile DRAM.

Beyond Apple, the Samsung MX (mobile experience) division — structurally separate from Samsung's memory business — purchased LPDDR5X for the Galaxy S series and the broader Android flagship tier. Xiaomi, OPPO, Vivo, and Google Pixel represented the next tier of mobile DRAM volume. The mobile segment as a whole had contracted sharply through 2022 and 2023 as smartphone unit volumes fell and the post-COVID inventory correction ran through the channel; by fiscal 2024, mobile DRAM was recovering but remained a lower-margin segment relative to the HBM and server DRAM tiers.

## Graphics DRAM, Automotive, and Solidigm Enterprise SSD

GDDR6X and GDDR7 memory for discrete GPU cards — NVIDIA GeForce and AMD Radeon — represented a third tier of DRAM revenue, primarily serving the gaming and consumer AI inference market. This segment's pricing dynamics tracked the gaming market cycle more closely than the data-centre cycle and did not carry the structural premium of HBM.

Automotive DRAM and NAND represented an early-stage but strategically significant customer category. Tesla, BYD, and the broader Chinese EV OEM ecosystem, alongside European and Japanese manufacturers procuring through Tier 1 automotive suppliers, required DRAM and NAND qualified to the AEC-Q100 automotive reliability standard. The automotive memory market was in a multi-year ramp through 2024, with per-vehicle memory content increasing as advanced driver-assistance systems and in-vehicle infotainment platforms became standard equipment.

Solidigm — the ~~San Jose-headquartered~~ ==Rancho Cordova, California-headquartered== SSD subsidiary SK Hynix acquired through the two-phase USD 9 billion Intel NAND deal, with phase one closing December 2021 — supplied enterprise NVMe SSDs to the hyperscaler data-centre build-out. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta were the principal Solidigm enterprise customers, and the SSD content intensity of AI-training cluster builds had increased materially through 2023 and 2024 as the volume of training data and checkpoint-storage requirements expanded. ~~Rob Crooke, who had led Intel's Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group before the divestiture, continued as Solidigm CEO through the snapshot date.~~ ==Rob Crooke, who had led Intel's Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group before the divestiture, served as Solidigm's launch-era CEO; by May 2023, David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh had been appointed co-CEOs and remained in those roles through the snapshot date.== The Dalian, China fab remained the principal NAND wafer-manufacturing site for Solidigm — a geopolitical exposure discussed below.

## Equipment Supply Chain: Structural Dependencies

SK Hynix operates as an integrated device manufacturer, meaning it executes wafer fabrication, packaging, and test internally without dependency on external foundries for memory production. This vertical integration distinguishes the memory IDM model from the fabless-foundry model prevalent in logic semiconductors.

Within the IDM structure, SK Hynix carries concentrated equipment supplier dependencies that are broadly shared across the memory industry. ASML's extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems are essential to the advanced DRAM process nodes deployed at Icheon and Cheongju — a dependency that intensified with each successive technology node reduction. Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, and Tokyo Electron supply the deposition, etch, and inspection equipment that the broader fab ecosystem requires.

Silicon wafer supply for SK Hynix's Korean fabs draws on SUMCO, Shin-Etsu Chemical, and SK Siltron — the last of which is itself an SK Group subsidiary, representing a degree of vertical integration into upstream materials that the broader group structure facilitates. Advanced packaging supply for HBM — specifically the through-silicon via interconnect and thermal compression bonding materials — represents a more specialised and tighter supply constraint. The rapid scaling of HBM output through 2023 and 2024 created intermittent constraints in TSV packaging consumables and bonding equipment capacity that the broader supply chain was still absorbing.

## Geopolitical Exposure: Wuxi and Dalian

SK Hynix's China-based manufacturing carried the most concentrated geopolitical risk in the company's asset base. The Wuxi DRAM fab — a legacy asset from the pre-SK Group Hynix era — represented a meaningful share of older-generation DRAM wafer output. The Dalian fab, acquired as part of the Solidigm transaction, produced NAND wafers for the enterprise SSD business.

US export control expansions through 2022, 2023, and 2024 progressively restricted the transfer of advanced semiconductor equipment to China-based fabs. SK Hynix secured a renewable one-year exemption from the US Commerce Department's October 2022 export control rule that permitted continued equipment supply to its Wuxi facility; the exemption was subsequently renewed, and the company managed the constraint by directing advanced-node investment to its Korean facilities while running Wuxi on the installed base. The Korean government's active engagement with Washington on behalf of Korean IDMs — SK Hynix and Samsung — reflected the broader industrial policy priority the Korean state assigned to maintaining the competitiveness of its principal technology exporters. Korean CHIPS-equivalent support frameworks, including tax credit mechanisms and infrastructure co-investment programmes, provided domestic capex support for the sustained investment cycle the HBM buildout required.

The net effect of the geopolitical constraint was to accelerate the bifurcation of SK Hynix's capital allocation: leading-edge investment concentrated in Korea, with China assets managed at steady-state until regulatory clarity or divestiture provided a resolution path. By the snapshot date, no definitive announcement on the disposition of the Wuxi or Dalian assets had been made.

chapters.title: Samsung, Micron, Kioxia, and the HBM share war
chapters.body:
## The Triopoly Remapped

For most of the twenty-first century, the global DRAM industry ran on a simple axis: Samsung Electronics led, SK Hynix followed, and Micron Technology occupied a distant third position defined by its Idaho cost structure and US customer relationships. [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com) and [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com) industry surveys published through 2022 placed Samsung at roughly 40–44 percent of global DRAM revenue, SK Hynix at 27–30 percent, and Micron at 20–24 percent — a triopoly stable enough to be almost geological. The emergence of high-bandwidth memory as the critical component in artificial intelligence accelerators fractured that stability and produced the most significant competitive redistribution in semiconductor memory since the Japanese industry's collapse in the early 1990s.

~~By the close of fiscal 2024~~ ==By the first quarter of 2025, on TrendForce's tally ($9.72 billion versus Samsung's $9.1 billion)==, SK Hynix had displaced Samsung as the revenue-leading DRAM supplier. It had not done so by closing the gap in commodity server or PC DRAM — Samsung retained its scale and cost advantages in those segments. It had done so by winning the single most valuable sub-market in the industry's history: the principal supply position for NVIDIA's HBM-stacked accelerators, first across the H100 and H200 series and then across the Blackwell B100, B200, and GB200 generations. The financial consequences were visible in the headline print: SK Hynix reported fiscal 2024 revenue of approximately KRW 66.2 trillion (roughly USD 50 billion), more than double the KRW 32.8 trillion of the prior year, with operating profit recovering to KRW 23.5 trillion from a KRW 7.7 trillion operating loss in fiscal 2023 — a swing of approximately KRW 31 trillion in a single fiscal year.

## Samsung: The Principal Challenger

Samsung Electronics' memory business has operated from a position of structural dominance for decades, built on process-technology leadership, vertically integrated manufacturing, and the scale advantage of running both the world's largest foundry and its largest memory operation under a single capital allocation framework. That structural position did not collapse in 2024; it was selectively outflanked.

The specific failure point was HBM3E qualification at NVIDIA. Industry reporting from [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com), [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com), and [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com) documented through 2024 and into 2025 that Samsung's HBM3E product had encountered yield and thermal performance challenges that prevented it from clearing NVIDIA's certification standards in volume. NVIDIA publicly declined to confirm or deny supplier-specific qualification status, as is standard practice, but the supply chain consequences were legible: SK Hynix continued to ship the overwhelming majority of the HBM stacks populating NVIDIA's Blackwell-generation products, while Samsung's contribution to that product family remained limited.

The qualification difficulty was consequential in absolute dollar terms. HBM commands a substantial premium over commodity DRAM — industry analysts at [TrendForce](https://www.trendforce.com) estimated in 2024 that HBM ASPs were running five to eight times the equivalent die area in standard DDR5 DRAM — and NVIDIA's accelerator volumes had scaled dramatically with AI infrastructure spending by Microsoft Azure, AWS, Meta, and Google. A supplier unable to clear NVIDIA's HBM3E certification was excluded from the highest-value demand pocket in the industry's history.

Samsung's strategic response was to accelerate its HBM4 development programme and to seek broader qualification across alternative AI accelerator customers, including Google's TPU programme and AMD's MI-series. HBM4 represents the next node transition — wider bus interface, higher bandwidth per stack, with SK Hynix and Samsung both targeting volume production on roughly parallel timelines. For Samsung, HBM4 is the principal re-entry vector. Whether it can close the yield and thermal reliability gap that produced the HBM3E difficulties, or whether SK Hynix's process maturity in stacked DRAM production will sustain the lead into the next generation, is the central unresolved competitive question facing both companies as of the May 2026 snapshot date.

## Micron: The Incremental Insurgent

Micron Technology's position in the HBM market is categorically different from Samsung's. Samsung was the expected HBM3E challenger — the company with the process scale and capital base to contest SK Hynix's lead. Micron entered the HBM3E market as an incremental supplier rather than a principal one, securing qualification with NVIDIA for the Blackwell cycle but shipping substantially smaller volumes than SK Hynix.

The strategic significance of Micron's HBM entry is nevertheless real. Micron brings a distinct set of structural advantages: its Boise, Idaho manufacturing base qualifies for US CHIPS Act subsidies and positions the company as the preferred domestic HBM supplier for US government-adjacent AI infrastructure procurement. The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 directed approximately USD 52 billion toward domestic semiconductor manufacturing investment, and Micron has been among the principal beneficiaries — the company announced a multi-billion-dollar Boise and New York capacity expansion programme supported by direct CHIPS Act grants.

| Metric | SK Hynix | Samsung | Micron |
|---|---|---|---|
| ~~DRAM revenue rank (FY2024 est.)~~ ==DRAM revenue rank (1Q25, TrendForce)== | 1st | 2nd | 3rd |
| HBM3E principal NVIDIA supplier | ✓ | ✗ (qualification difficulties) | Partial |
| HBM4 volume readiness | Lead | Challenger | Emerging |
| US CHIPS Act manufacturing | No | ~~No~~ ==Yes (up to $4.745bn, Taylor/Austin, TX)== | Yes |
| Fab geography | Icheon / Cheongju (KR), Wuxi (CN) | Pyeongtaek (KR), Xi'an (CN) | Boise / NY (US), Japan |

Micron's incremental HBM position creates an optionality that matters disproportionately to US policy risk scenarios. If US export controls on advanced AI chips to China tighten further, the reshoring of HBM supply to American fabs acquires strategic as well as commercial significance. For SK Hynix, Micron's CHIPS Act positioning is a longer-term competitive pressure that does not displace its current NVIDIA supply relationship but represents a structural backstop for any customer or regulatory scenario in which geographic diversification of AI memory supply becomes a procurement priority. Samsung's own CHIPS Act award for Taylor and Austin, by contrast, anchors a logic and foundry expansion rather than a domestic HBM line, so the US-reshored HBM contest as of the snapshot date remains a Micron-versus-imported-supply question.

## The NAND Battlefield: Kioxia, SanDisk, and Solidigm

The NAND flash market operates under a different competitive logic. Where DRAM has consolidated into a tight triopoly, NAND retains a fragmented quintopoly — Samsung, Kioxia, SK Hynix (operating its enterprise NAND franchise through the Solidigm subsidiary), Western Digital (separating its NAND operation as standalone SanDisk), and Micron. Gross margins in commodity NAND have historically been lower and more volatile than in DRAM, and the market lacks a premium sub-segment analogous to HBM to generate the kind of outsized ASP uplift that reshaped the DRAM economics in 2024.

Kioxia — the former Toshiba Memory Corporation, spun off from Toshiba in 2017 following Toshiba's accounting crisis and listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2024 — occupies the number-two global NAND position by share. [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com) reported Kioxia's IPO in late 2024 at a market capitalisation of approximately JPY 750 billion (roughly USD 5 billion at the time of listing), a substantial discount to its prior private valuation. Kioxia competes primarily in commodity 3D NAND across mobile, consumer, and enterprise client SSD segments. It is absent from the HBM market.

SK Hynix's Solidigm subsidiary, the enterprise SSD and NAND business acquired from Intel in a two-phase transaction closing between ~~December 2021 and late 2025~~ ==December 29, 2021 and March 27, 2025== for approximately USD 9 billion in total consideration, repositioned SK Hynix as a serious competitor in enterprise NVMe SSDs. Solidigm, headquartered in ~~San Jose and led by Rob Crooke — formerly Intel's senior vice president and general manager of the Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group~~ ==Rancho Cordova, California and led since May 2023 by co-CEOs David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh==, competes directly against Samsung's 990 Pro and PM9A3 enterprise SSD lines, Western Digital's enterprise NVMe portfolio, and pure-play enterprise storage vendors including Pure Storage. The Solidigm acquisition was strategically significant for two reasons beyond the immediate NAND share: it transferred the Dalian, China NAND wafer fabrication assets into SK Hynix's supply base, and it granted SK Hynix the Intel NAND IP stack needed to compete in QLC-heavy enterprise workloads where Samsung had previously been dominant.

## China's Captive Insurgency

Any competitive assessment of the memory industry requires acknowledgment of the domestic Chinese suppliers, even though their global competitive reach remains constrained. ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) has emerged as a credible producer of commodity LPDDR4 and DDR4 DRAM, serving the domestic Chinese smartphone and PC market. Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC) reached 128-layer 3D NAND production maturity before the US Bureau of Industry and Security added YMTC to the Entity List in December 2022, restricting its access to advanced US semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

The export control framework that governs Chinese memory — including the October 2022 and subsequent rounds of US equipment export restrictions targeting advanced lithography and etch tools — has effectively capped CXMT and YMTC at process nodes trailing the global frontier by two to three generations. Neither company is a credible competitor in HBM. YMTC has maintained its domestic NAND position behind the Great Firewall, and its Xtacking 3D architecture has been viewed with technical respect by industry analysts at [DigiTimes](https://www.digitimes.com), but its global market access is structurally constrained as long as US export controls remain in force. For SK Hynix, the Chinese capacity overhang represents a commodity pricing risk in NAND — particularly in mobile and consumer segments — rather than a direct HBM competitive threat.

## The Durability Question

Three structural questions frame the competitive outlook at the May 2026 snapshot date.

The first is whether SK Hynix can sustain its HBM leadership through the HBM4 cycle. The company's advantage in HBM3E was built on earlier investment in through-silicon-via stacking expertise, thermally stable dielectric materials, and the close engineering co-development relationship with NVIDIA. Samsung's HBM4 programme is its most focused remediation effort; the question is whether the yield and thermal reliability challenges that caused the HBM3E setbacks were addressable at the engineering level or reflect deeper architectural differences in how the two companies approach stacked DRAM. If Samsung resolves those issues with HBM4, the competitive dynamic reverts toward a two-supplier market at NVIDIA. If the difficulties persist, SK Hynix's lead extends into the Rubin and beyond-Rubin NVIDIA roadmap.

The second is whether Micron's incremental HBM share and its CHIPS Act manufacturing backstop expand into a more meaningful competitive position. The US reshoring incentive structure and the strategic premium placed on domestic AI supply chain security by US government procurement could accelerate Micron's HBM capacity build faster than market economics alone would justify. Micron's Boise HBM expansion timeline and the CHIPS Act capital deployment schedule will be the leading indicators.

The third is whether the 2024 operating profit recovery — KRW 23.5 trillion on revenue of KRW 66.2 trillion — represents a durable structural improvement in memory industry economics or a cyclical peak inflated by the AI infrastructure investment surge. The historical memory cycle has been defined by overcapacity, price collapse, and loss-cycle trough; the AI demand wave has structurally shifted the server DRAM and HBM demand floor, but commodity DRAM and NAND pricing remained subject to the same supply-discipline dynamics that have defined the industry for four decades. Whether AI demand is large enough to permanently suppress the cycle's volatility, or whether it merely introduced a new premium segment atop an unchanged commodity substrate, is the question that will determine whether the 2024 print is a new baseline or a peak.

chapters.title: From 2023 losses to the 2024 record and the HBM4 race
chapters.body:
## The bottom of the cycle

Few companies in the global semiconductor industry have experienced a reversal as violent as the one SK Hynix navigated between 2022 and 2024. The company that posted KRW 6.81 trillion in operating profit for fiscal 2022 recorded a KRW 7.73 trillion operating *loss* one year later — a swing of more than KRW 14 trillion in a single annual reporting cycle. Revenue fell from KRW 44.62 trillion to KRW 32.77 trillion, the steepest single-year revenue contraction in the company's post-workout history. Every major product segment — conventional DRAM, server DRAM, and NAND flash — faced simultaneous oversupply as the post-pandemic inventory correction ran deeper and longer than most forecasters had anticipated.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (KRW T) | Revenue (~USD B) | Operating Profit / (Loss) (KRW T) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 44.62 | ~33 | 6.81 |
| 2023 | 32.77 | ~25 | (7.73) |
| 2024 | 66.19 | ~50 | 23.47 |

*Source: [SK Hynix IR — Financial Information](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information); SEC EDGAR CIK 0001687247*

The signals had arrived late in 2022. PC shipments collapsed following the pandemic pull-forward; hyperscale data-centre operators worked down the excess DRAM and NAND they had accumulated during the supply-constrained years of 2021 and early 2022; and consumer electronics demand softened across every geography. What made the 2023 downturn structurally different from prior memory troughs was its breadth: there was no product segment offering a cyclical offset.

## An acquisition into the storm

SK Hynix absorbed the worst of the downturn while simultaneously integrating what had been, at announcement, one of the largest semiconductor acquisitions in Korean corporate history. On 20 October 2020, the company agreed with Intel Corporation to acquire Intel's NAND memory and storage business — including the Dalian, China fabrication complex — for approximately USD 9 billion, structured across two closing phases. The strategic rationale was scale: NAND flash was Samsung-dominated, and the Intel portfolio offered a ready-made enterprise SSD customer base alongside an established client-storage product line that SK Hynix lacked internally.

Phase one closed on 29 December 2021, transferring the NAND SSD business and Dalian assets into a newly formed subsidiary, Solidigm Technology, headquartered in ~~San Jose~~ ==Rancho Cordova==, California. [Rob Crooke](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/press-releases), formerly Intel's Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Non-Volatile Memory Solutions Group, stayed to lead Solidigm — providing operational continuity across the transition. The same month, Park Jung-ho was confirmed as SK Hynix Vice Chairman and CEO, creating a unified leadership mandate to run the integration alongside the company's existing DRAM and nascent HBM strategy.

The timing proved punishing. Solidigm launched into the front edge of the sharpest NAND price decline in cycle history. Enterprise SSD average selling prices fell sharply through 2022 and into 2023, compressing Solidigm's margins against a Dalian fixed-cost base that could not be quickly reduced. Phase two of the acquisition — covering residual wafer-supply intellectual property and additional manufacturing operations — was structured for a closing ~~targeted around December 2025~~ ==targeted for March 2025==, creating an integration overhang that persisted across the depth of the memory downturn.

## The HBM pivot

While conventional memory revenues deteriorated through 2023, a structurally distinct revenue stream was beginning to emerge. SK Hynix had been developing high-bandwidth memory technology through the prior half-decade, and the commercial demand pull arrived in the form of NVIDIA's H100 accelerator — the GPU that became the essential compute substrate for large-language-model training following the ChatGPT inflection of late 2022.

The H100 required HBM3 memory stacks at its core. SK Hynix was, by the second half of 2023, the principal qualified supplier of HBM3 to [NVIDIA](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/press-releases). Samsung Electronics, despite commanding the largest DRAM manufacturing footprint in the world, encountered qualification delays on HBM3 that prevented it from supplying at commercial volume for the H100 cycle. The competitive consequence was decisive: SK Hynix absorbed the majority of NVIDIA's HBM3 volume as H100 production scaled rapidly to meet data-centre demand, even as the broader DRAM and NAND books remained deeply in loss.

The HBM premium — a per-gigabyte average selling price that commands a substantial multiple above conventional DRAM, reflecting the complexity of through-silicon via stacking, thermal management, and tight customer-specific qualification requirements — meant that even modest HBM revenue was highly accretive to the operating line. HBM3 revenue in the second half of 2023 did not erase the annual loss, but it interrupted the trajectory and signalled the character of the recovery to come.

## The 2024 record

The first quarter of 2024 marked the inflection point. SK Hynix returned to operating profitability as HBM revenue scaled, DRAM spot prices recovered off their cycle lows, and NAND conditions began to stabilise. The quarterly progression through the year was steep and consistent; by the second half, SK Hynix was posting quarterly results that exceeded any prior full-year operating profit in the company's history.

In March 2024, SK Hynix announced ~~the CEO transition~~ ==a leadership-structure change== that had been prepared within the company's leadership structure. Park Jung-ho, who had overseen the Intel NAND acquisition and had made the sustained commitment to HBM investment that now defined the company's commercial position, ~~ceded the CEO role to Kwak Noh-Jung~~ ==stepped back from his co-CEO position, leaving Kwak Noh-Jung — who had been appointed President & CEO alongside Park in March 2022 — as sole chief executive==. Kwak had joined SK Hynix in 1994 and spent more than three decades in semiconductor manufacturing roles, most recently as President and Chief Production Officer — the company's senior manufacturing executive. He holds a doctorate in ~~electrical engineering from KAIST~~ ==Materials Engineering from Korea University==. Park continued as Vice Chairman, preserving strategic continuity at the moment when the HBM ramp required both the framework Park had constructed and the manufacturing execution depth that Kwak's career had been built around.

Kwak, speaking ~~at his appointment in~~ ==in== March 2024, framed the mandate in operational terms: the priority was sustaining HBM technology leadership and extending that advantage through successive generations. The language was measured, as it consistently would be through his early tenure — the temperament of a manufacturing engineer rather than a dealmaker.

HBM3E, the next-generation specification required for NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture — the B100, B200, and GB200 accelerator systems that represented NVIDIA's largest product cycle to date — went into volume production through 2024 with SK Hynix as the principal supplier. The Blackwell ramp drove the second half's record results. For fiscal 2024, [SK Hynix reported](https://www.skhynix.com/eng/ir/financial-information) revenue of KRW 66.19 trillion (~USD 50 billion) and operating profit of KRW 23.47 trillion — the KRW 31.2 trillion year-on-year swing representing the largest single-year earnings recovery in the company's recorded history.

## Samsung's stumble and the share war

The qualification gap between SK Hynix and Samsung on HBM became the defining competitive dynamic of the cycle. Samsung encountered repeated yield and thermal-management challenges with its HBM3E product that prevented qualification at commercial volume for NVIDIA's Blackwell platform during the core 2024 ramp. Micron Technology, which had developed its own HBM3E architecture and accelerated investment after observing SK Hynix's qualification success, began qualifying for NVIDIA and captured a meaningful but smaller share than SK Hynix. For much of the critical 2024 Blackwell ramp, the supplier base was effectively SK Hynix-primary with Micron as a secondary source — and Samsung absent.

The structural inversion was striking against the prior decade's competitive hierarchy. Samsung's scale in DRAM had historically conferred cost and yield advantages that made it the default choice for volume compute memory. On HBM, the qualification requirements proved more complex than scale alone addressed: thermal uniformity across 12-layer stacks, through-silicon via precision, and integration specifications tightly bound to NVIDIA's CoWoS packaging required process maturity that SK Hynix had built specifically for this product family over years of investment. Samsung's eventual qualification — delayed but expected — remained the outstanding competitive variable through the snapshot period.

## Into HBM4: The Rubin race

By 2025, competitive attention had shifted to HBM4, the next-generation specification designed for NVIDIA's Rubin architecture and subsequent platforms. SK Hynix began shipping HBM4 engineering samples in 2025 and entered qualification work with NVIDIA targeting the Rubin generation supply position. HBM4's technical demands differed from its predecessors in a structurally significant respect: the base logic die at the foundation of the memory stack would be produced using a leading-edge logic process rather than a standard memory node, requiring coordination with an external foundry partner. This introduced a supply-chain complexity — and a new inter-company dependency — absent from prior HBM generations.

The qualification race for Rubin-generation HBM4 was, as of the snapshot date, unresolved. Samsung, motivated by the commercial cost of its HBM3E delay, had intensified its HBM4 development program. Micron, having established its NVIDIA beachhead through HBM3E, was pursuing parallel HBM4 qualification. Each successive HBM generation resets the qualification clock, which is both the mechanism that has sustained SK Hynix's lead — process knowledge built through prior qualification cycles is transferable — and the vulnerability that Samsung and Micron's engineering investments are targeting.

## Forward catalysts

From the snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the near-term catalyst set for SK Hynix encompassed first-quarter 2026 earnings results and the quarterly HBM revenue disclosure; any formal NVIDIA confirmation of HBM4 qualification for the Rubin platform; the trajectory of HBM4 mass-production ramp economics and yield; conventional DRAM and NAND pricing through the broader memory cycle; and the operational performance of Solidigm following the phase-two close of the Intel NAND acquisition, ~~which had been targeted for December 2025~~ ==which closed on 27 March 2025 for approximately USD 1.9 billion==. Solidigm's full integration — once the residual wafer-supply IP and manufacturing operations transferred — would resolve the long-running structural uncertainty around the subsidiary's cost base and strategic positioning within a NAND market that had itself undergone significant consolidation since the acquisition announcement.

The durability of the HBM premium across a 2026 in which multiple qualified suppliers are competing for Rubin-generation allocation is the core investor question. SK Hynix's commercial argument rests on the proposition that each qualification cycle compounds process advantage — that being first, repeatedly, at each HBM generation creates a margin and volume buffer that persists until competitors close the technical gap. Whether that advantage is measured in quarters or years will determine whether the 2024 record print is the beginning of a sustained earnings plateau or the peak of a cycle that normalises as Samsung and Micron qualify at scale.

## Specialist and social commentary

Specialist commentary framing of SK Hynix by Aleabit was not surfaced in the bounded primary-source set.

Within the broader community of semiconductor analysts active on X and specialist platforms through 2024–2025, the dominant debate concerned the duration of SK Hynix's NVIDIA qualification advantage. Bullish framing emphasised the generational reset logic: HBM4's base-die complexity raised the qualification bar further, potentially extending the lead rather than compressing it. Bearish framing focused on the pace of Samsung's corrective investment — the company had publicly committed to resolving HBM3E yield issues — and on Micron's rising share as evidence that supply-base normalisation was already under way. The comment shared across most informed positions was that 2024's KRW 23.47 trillion operating profit was real and credible; the disagreement was whether it marked a new earnings floor or a cycle peak that mean-reversion would test as HBM4 volume ramped across a broader supplier base.

chapters.title: HBM TSV packaging, EUV DRAM, and the technology roadmap
chapters.body:
## Through-Silicon Via: The Crown Jewel of the HBM Franchise

SK Hynix's competitive position in the high bandwidth memory market rests on a single, extraordinarily difficult manufacturing capability: the through-silicon via. TSV technology — the practice of drilling vertical holes through individual DRAM dies and filling them with conductive copper pillars to create a direct electrical pathway between stacked chips — demands tolerances measured in microns and thermal management solutions that have eluded mass-volume competitors for years.

The company's HBM3 product, which began volume shipments to NVIDIA in 2023, stacks 12 DRAM dies atop a logic base die. Each die is thinned to below 30 microns before TSV formation, and the finished stack is bonded through thermal compression and non-conductive film adhesive in a process that can consume several hours per unit. Yield management at this scale separates SK Hynix from Samsung Electronics' HBM3 product, which experienced well-documented qualification difficulties at NVIDIA through much of 2024 — a gap that translated directly into SK Hynix's dominant share of HBM revenue across that period.

HBM3E, which entered volume production at the Icheon facility in the first half of 2024, retained the 12-high stack architecture but pushed per-pin bandwidth to 9.8 gigabits per second, delivering an aggregate bandwidth per package of approximately 1.2 terabytes per second. The principal engineering challenge in the transition was managing heat flux through a taller, denser stack operating at higher frequencies — a problem SK Hynix addressed through refinements to the thermal interface material between dies and an updated underfill dispensing process. NVIDIA's H200 and Blackwell-architecture accelerators shipped with SK Hynix HBM3E as the primary memory supplier, a relationship that underpinned the KRW 23.4 trillion operating profit SK Hynix reported for fiscal 2024.

## HBM4 and the 16-High Stack

SK Hynix confirmed its HBM4 development roadmap through investor briefings and earnings communications in 2024 and into 2025. The target architecture moves from 12-high to 16-high die stacking — a 33 percent increase in stacked dies per package — while maintaining a footprint compatible with next-generation AI accelerator substrate designs.

The technical demands of 16-high HBM4 are substantially greater than the HBM3E transition. Thinner individual dies increase susceptibility to warpage during bonding; the additional four layers compound cumulative thermal resistance through the stack, requiring advances in heat dissipation via the TSV columns themselves and, potentially, through liquid-cooling integration at the package level. SK Hynix has publicly discussed embedded cooling channels within the HBM4 package as part of longer-term co-packaging research conducted alongside TSMC and in alignment with NVIDIA system-level memory specifications.

Power efficiency is the other principal HBM4 design vector. As AI training clusters scale to hundreds of thousands of accelerators, the HBM subsystem's energy draw becomes a meaningful fraction of total data-centre power consumption. SK Hynix engineers targeted double-digit percentage improvements in picojoules-per-bit versus HBM3E as a baseline requirement for HBM4 customer qualification — a metric that has become as commercially decisive as raw bandwidth for hyperscale buyers negotiating total cost of ownership at rack scale.

## EUV DRAM and Node Migration

Alongside HBM, SK Hynix's broader DRAM roadmap pivoted structurally toward extreme ultraviolet lithography. The company introduced EUV patterning into volume DRAM production at the 1a-nanometre node — broadly characterised as sub-15nm half-pitch — enabling finer cell definition without the multi-patterning complexity that had throttled yields under immersion ArF-based processes at tighter geometries.

Subsequent node generations deepened EUV penetration. The 1b-nm node, which entered production during 2023–24, expanded EUV exposure layers beyond the single critical-layer insertion of 1a-nm. The 1c-nm node, in active development across the snapshot window, was expected to deploy EUV across a broader set of interconnect and active-area layers, further compressing bit cost and improving power characteristics per gigabit. SK Hynix's DRAM capital expenditure disclosures in its 2024 annual filings reflected this trajectory, with a material share of fab equipment spend attributable to ASML EUV scanner installations at the Icheon M16 facility.

The financial significance of this migration is direct: lower bit cost at each successive node is the primary mechanism by which SK Hynix translates volume growth into margin expansion. Management has identified EUV yield maturation as the principal variable governing the pace of DRAM cost reduction through the near term — a dynamic that also constrains the speed at which Samsung and Micron can narrow the cost gap.

## Mobile, Graphics, and Adjacent DRAM

LPDDR5X reached volume production for the principal smartphone customers — Apple, Samsung's mobile division, Qualcomm-platform handset makers, and Google — as the performance tier of choice for flagship handsets. SK Hynix positioned LPDDR6, the next-generation JEDEC specification targeting approximately 10.7 gigabits per second per pin, as a 2026-onwards product in alignment with the standardisation timeline, with early engagement from Apple and Qualcomm Snapdragon platform customers.

In graphics DRAM, SK Hynix supplied GDDR6 and GDDR6X into NVIDIA GeForce and AMD Radeon discrete GPU platforms across the current generation. GDDR7, standardised by JEDEC at data rates beginning at 32 gigabits per second, entered SK Hynix production qualification in 2024–25 for next-generation discrete GPUs, broadening addressable revenue per graphics card alongside the shift of AI inference workloads from HBM-based accelerators to lower-cost GDDR7-equipped hardware.

## 3D NAND: 238-Layer and the Solidigm Architecture Bifurcation

SK Hynix's NAND business occupies a structurally distinct competitive position from DRAM. The company's 238-layer charge-trap-based 3D NAND entered volume production and was deployed into consumer SSDs, mobile storage, and enterprise drives. Layer count is a partial indicator of competitiveness; SK Hynix emphasised cell reliability and read latency alongside raw layer count in customer qualification programmes.

The 2021 acquisition of Intel's NAND and SSD business — completed in two tranches, with the Dalian, China fabrication facility transferred in ~~the first quarter of 2025~~ ==phase one on December 29, 2021 alongside Intel's SSD business== — added a qualitatively distinct technology lineage: Intel's floating-gate 3D NAND architecture. Floating-gate cells store charge through a different physical mechanism compared to charge-trap designs and have historically been associated with stronger endurance in enterprise and data-centre workloads. SK Hynix, operating this IP through the Solidigm subsidiary headquartered in ~~San Jose~~ ==Rancho Cordova, California==, thereby gained the ability to serve customers with competing architectural preferences — an unusual bifurcation in a market where most suppliers are committed to a single cell technology and one that has supported Solidigm's enterprise SSD positioning with Microsoft Azure, AWS, and Meta.

## CIS and the Residual Sensor Portfolio

CMOS image sensors constitute a smaller but strategically maintained segment. SK Hynix's CIS production served smartphone manufacturers requiring stacked sensor architectures for front and rear camera modules, targeting the mid-tier and cost-competitive handset OEM segment below the Samsung LSI and Sony Semiconductor Solutions high-end tier. The CIS business did not receive the same capital intensity as DRAM or HBM but provided incremental fab utilisation across advanced process nodes.

## R&D Commitment and Patent Density

SK Hynix's research and development expenditure ran at approximately KRW 4–5 trillion annually in recent periods, representing high single-digit percentages of revenue. The commitment was directed overwhelmingly toward HBM packaging integration, EUV DRAM node development, and next-generation NAND architecture — categories where intellectual property depth compounds into yield advantage across multiple product cycles.

The patent portfolio spans DRAM cell design, TSV formation and bonding processes, HBM thermal management, NAND cell architecture, and memory controller interface standards. In TSV-specific packaging, the breadth and seniority of SK Hynix filings across the USPTO and Korean Intellectual Property Office constitute a meaningful barrier to rapid competitive replication. Kwak Noh-jung, addressing investors following the company's fourth-quarter 2024 results, characterised the accumulated HBM packaging know-how as a structural advantage built over more than a decade of sustained engineering investment — one that product-cycle imitation alone cannot quickly close.

chapters.title: Memory cycle, Samsung HBM4 push, China exposure, Korean chaebol governance
chapters.body:
## The cycle that giveth

No investor in SK Hynix can afford to read the KRW 23.47 trillion operating profit of fiscal 2024 without also memorising the KRW 7.73 trillion operating loss of fiscal 2023. The same memory cycle that produced the steepest single-year recovery in the company's recorded history — a KRW 31 trillion swing in twelve months — had, the year before, produced a loss nearly as large as the SK Group paid to acquire the entire company in 2012. The velocity in both directions is the point. Memory pricing is set at the intersection of capital-intensive, multi-year capacity decisions and demand that shifts on quarters, not years. Post-COVID inventory correction, compounded by the gap between AI infrastructure pre-spending and actual memory demand, drove pricing to levels that erased years of profit in a single cycle. The 2024 recovery was real and substantial, but the structural dynamics of the industry have not changed. Commodity DRAM capacity from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron continues to grow; if AI infrastructure spending moderates or the server refresh cycle pauses, the margin on conventional DRAM compresses first, and HBM pricing — still partially shielded by qualification barriers — faces pressure with a lag.

Near-term, SK Hynix carries meaningful mitigants: a product mix increasingly weighted to HBM3E, where it holds the principal NVIDIA qualification and the associated margin premium; and a diversified revenue base across mobile DRAM, server DRAM, and Solidigm NAND that provides some buffer against any single end-market deterioration. The medium-term concern is structural: the 2024 profit print will attract capital. Samsung has already communicated capacity expansion plans. If the AI infrastructure buildout that created the HBM supercycle moderates before the next cycle inflection, SK Hynix re-enters the commodity portion of the cycle with a heavily capitalised balance sheet and the same cyclical exposure it has always carried.

## Samsung's structural comeback bid

The single most important competitive fact in the memory industry through 2024 and into 2025 was not a product launch or a capacity decision. It was a qualification failure. Samsung Electronics, which holds a larger overall DRAM capacity base than SK Hynix and has historically dominated the server DRAM market by scale, failed to qualify its HBM3E product at NVIDIA on the thermal and yield parameters required for the Blackwell generation of AI accelerators. SK Hynix stepped into that gap, became the principal scaled HBM3E supplier across Blackwell B100, B200, and GB200, and earned the pricing premium that drove the 2024 operating-profit recovery.

Samsung's structural resources — its Device Solutions division, its broader semiconductor manufacturing scale, and its captive memory architecture investment — mean the question is not whether Samsung re-enters the HBM qualification race but on what timeline and at which node. HBM4, the next-generation architecture targeting NVIDIA's Rubin platform, resets the qualification competition. Samsung has disclosed active HBM4 development; its scale advantage in advanced DRAM provides the capital base to pursue multiple architectural approaches in parallel. The near-term mitigant for SK Hynix is that HBM qualification at NVIDIA involves thermal, yield, and integration-level testing that historically takes multiple quarters once samples are submitted — Samsung must clear those gates before it can ship at volume. A qualification delay into 2026 or beyond would preserve SK Hynix's Rubin revenue base.

The medium-term concern is that Samsung's failure at HBM3E was an execution problem, not a fundamental architectural one. The history of the memory industry is that scale advantages eventually reassert themselves. If Samsung resolves the thermal management and yield issues that impaired its HBM3E qualification and presents a competitive HBM4 product to NVIDIA and to the broader hyperscaler customer base — Microsoft Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud are all potential buyers at volume — SK Hynix's current revenue and margin premium compresses toward the historical norm. The strategic value of the HBM lead was always that it was temporary; the financial value of the 2024 print was that it arrived before the competition caught up. How long that lead persists into the HBM4 cycle is the central question for investors modelling the 2025-2026 period.

## Micron: the qualification principle in practice

Micron's progression through NVIDIA's HBM qualification process in 2024 and 2025 established a commercial principle that is as important as Samsung's catch-up bid: NVIDIA can and does re-allocate HBM share when execution warrants. Micron qualified its HBM3E product at NVIDIA and began shipping at commercial volumes — a smaller share of the Blackwell supply chain than SK Hynix, but a nonzero and growing one. The significance is not Micron's current share. It is the demonstration that a third qualified supplier exists and that NVIDIA has both the commercial incentive and the technical pathway to use it.

| Supplier | HBM3E NVIDIA Status (as of snapshot) | HBM4 Position |
|---|---|---|
| SK Hynix | Principal scaled supplier — B100/B200/GB200 | Targeting principal supplier for Rubin |
| Samsung | HBM3E qualification impaired | Active HBM4 development |
| Micron | Qualified, commercial volumes | HBM4 development disclosed |

Micron's manufacturing base in the United States — its Boise, Idaho fabs and the expanding facilities in Idaho, Virginia, and New York supported by CHIPS Act funding — gives it a geopolitical tailwind that ~~neither SK Hynix nor Samsung can match~~ ==SK Hynix cannot match, and that Samsung partially shares: a Samsung Electronics subsidiary was awarded up to $4.745 billion under the CHIPS and Science Act for Taylor and Austin, Texas semiconductor manufacturing and R&D capacity==. If US government procurement preferences or allied-nation supply-chain diversification requirements evolve in ways that favour domestically manufactured HBM, Micron's structural position improves independent of its product performance. The near-term mitigant is that yield and qualification timelines remain the binding constraints on HBM supply, and Micron has historically trailed on the advanced DRAM node transitions that underpin HBM stacking. The medium-term concern is cumulative share erosion: even at modest share gains per generation, a three-supplier HBM ecosystem dilutes the pricing power and margin premium that drove SK Hynix's 2024 recovery.

## China: the regulatory fault line

SK Hynix operates two principal manufacturing facilities on Chinese soil: a DRAM fab in Wuxi, Jiangsu Province — one of the company's most productive legacy DRAM facilities — and, through the Solidigm subsidiary, a NAND flash manufacturing facility in Dalian, Liaoning Province, acquired as part of the 2021 Intel NAND transaction. Both operations exist inside the evolving framework of US semiconductor export controls, and both represent a specific category of regulatory exposure that is not fully mitigable through commercial hedging.

The US CHIPS Act and the Commerce Department's export control framework have, since October 2022, progressively restricted the transfer of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China. SK Hynix received a temporary general licence permitting continued operation of its Wuxi and Dalian facilities while the policy framework stabilised. The operative risk is not the current licencing status — it is the trajectory of the policy. Each successive US-China trade and technology action since 2022 has tightened the perimeter around what equipment can be serviced, upgraded, or replaced at Chinese fabs. A facility that cannot receive advanced lithography equipment, etch tools, or deposition systems will, over a multi-year horizon, fall behind the technology curve relative to fabs operating without those restrictions.

The Dalian Solidigm facility carries an additional layer of complexity: it was acquired from Intel as part of a transaction that included NAND wafer-supply intellectual property and operational know-how. ~~The full close of that transaction was expected in late 2025~~ ==The second and final closing of that transaction occurred on March 27, 2025, for approximately $1.9 billion net of adjustments==; the status of IP transfers and operational integration at the Dalian facility in the context of US export controls remains a material consideration. ~~Rob Crooke, who leads Solidigm, built the Intel NAND business that Solidigm inherited, and his institutional knowledge of the Dalian operations is a stabilising factor.~~ ==Solidigm, headquartered in Rancho Cordova, California and led since May 2023 by co-CEOs David M. Dixon and Kevin Noh, inherited the Intel NAND organisation that includes the Dalian operations, and that operational continuity is a stabilising factor.== But no operational leadership substitutes for equipment access.

The near-term mitigant is that legacy-node DRAM and NAND manufacturing can continue at existing technology levels without new equipment at the relevant nodes. The medium-term concern is that "legacy node" becomes a longer-term competitive disadvantage as memory node transitions advance. If Wuxi cannot be upgraded from its current node through equipment restrictions, it produces an increasing cost and performance gap relative to SK Hynix's Korean fabs at Icheon and Cheongju.

## Governance: the chaebol structure and its investor implications

SK Hynix is not an independent company in the institutional sense that TSMC or Micron are. It is the principal semiconductor asset of the SK Group conglomerate, controlled through a cross-shareholding structure in which SK Inc. and ~~SK Telecom~~ ==SK Square== sit above the semiconductor subsidiary. ==SK Square holds 146,118,388 shares, or 20.5%, as the major shareholder on the snapshot-period ownership disclosure.== Choi Tae-won, the SK Group chairman, is the principal controlling shareholder through those intermediate holding structures.

For international investors accustomed to structures where capital allocation is determined by the board and management of the operating subsidiary, the chaebol model introduces a specific set of considerations. The controlling shareholder retains influence over capital allocation decisions — including whether SK Hynix's cash generation is deployed in semiconductor capacity expansion, dividends to minority shareholders, or cross-group financial support. The 2012 acquisition of Hynix by the SK Group was itself a capital allocation decision made at the conglomerate level, using SK Telecom as the lead acquirer. The 2021 Solidigm acquisition was executed while Park Jung-ho — a former SK Telecom CEO — held the SK Hynix chief executive role, a biographical fact that reflects the depth of group-level integration.

The ~~March 2024 CEO transition from Park Jung-ho to Kwak Noh-Jung was orderly and technically credentialled: Kwak holds a KAIST doctorate in electrical engineering and spent more than thirty years in SK Hynix's engineering and production organisation. Park continues as Vice Chairman, preserving institutional continuity.~~ ==March 2022 elevation of Kwak Noh-Jung to President & CEO, succeeding Park Jung-ho, was orderly and technically credentialled: Kwak holds a Ph.D. in Materials Engineering from Korea University and spent more than thirty years in SK Hynix's engineering and production organisation. A management-structure adjustment in March 2024 reframed the senior succession around Kwak, who has held the President & CEO title continuously since 2022.== The transition reflects the SK Group's practice of layered senior leadership rather than clean succession, a model that distributes formal authority across multiple senior figures while the controlling shareholder retains ultimate strategic direction. ==The current SK hynix board is chaired by independent director Ko Seung-Beom, with inside directors Kwak Noh-Jung and Cha Seon-Yong; Choi Tae-won exerts strategic influence through the SK Group holding structure rather than through a direct SK hynix board seat.==

For minority investors, the governance consideration is not acute but persistent: capital allocation, related-party transactions with SK Group affiliates, and strategic decisions about China manufacturing exposure will be made within a governance framework where the controlling shareholder's interests may not always align with minority return maximisation. Korean governance reforms and the Seoul Stock Exchange's corporate-value programme have, since 2023, provided incremental pressure on large-cap chaebol entities to improve minority return profiles. The question is whether that pressure is sufficient to fully align capital allocation with minority interests when the cycle turns and cash generation compresses.

## The AI capex dependency

The six categorical risks resolve to a single underlying dependency: SK Hynix's extraordinary 2024 results were a function of AI infrastructure capital expenditure at a scale and velocity that had no historical precedent. Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta committed, collectively, to hundreds of billions of dollars in data-centre buildout in 2023 and 2024, the majority of which required NVIDIA GPU clusters, and NVIDIA's GPU clusters required HBM at volumes that SK Hynix alone could supply at the required yield and specification. That dependency chain runs in both directions. Any moderation in hyperscaler AI capex — whether from regulatory pressure, return-on-investment recalibration, or a pause in the large-language-model scaling curve — translates directly into reduced NVIDIA GPU orders, which translates directly into reduced HBM demand, which compresses SK Hynix's revenue and margin toward the commodity DRAM baseline. The 2025 capex trajectories of the principal hyperscalers remained elevated at the snapshot date, but the history of infrastructure buildout cycles is that commitment and disbursement diverge when economic conditions shift. The structural HBM lead that Kwak Noh-Jung ~~inherited in March 2024~~ ==has stewarded since taking the CEO title in March 2022== was, at the snapshot date, intact. The risks catalogued in this chapter describe the conditions under which it might not remain so.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
The question that defines SK Hynix's forward calendar is narrow but consequentially large: can the company replicate, in the HBM4 cycle, the qualification-to-sole-supplier trajectory it ran with HBM3E through Blackwell? The KRW 23.47 trillion operating profit of fiscal 2024 — a KRW 31.2 trillion year-on-year swing from the 2023 trough — was substantially the harvest of a single structural moat: first and near-exclusive HBM qualification at NVIDIA across H100, H200, and the full Blackwell generation. The twelve months beginning May 2026 are the market's test of whether that moat is a structural property of the franchise or a cyclical artefact of Samsung's temporary disqualification.

## Quarterly Catalyst Calendar

**Late July 2026 — Q2 2026 earnings.** With Q1 2026 results already on the record as of the snapshot date, the July release is the first print expected to carry a meaningful HBM4 revenue contribution. SK Hynix guided in its April 2026 first-quarter earnings release toward HBM4 commercial shipment commencement in H1 2026 with volume ramp through the second half. The July print will answer three questions: whether HBM4 average selling prices are tracking above HBM3E exit levels; whether HBM revenue share within total DRAM mix is expanding toward the 40 per cent threshold consensus assumes for H2 2026; and whether conventional server DRAM pricing is providing underlying support or beginning a cyclical fade. The implicit competitive read — on whether Samsung has made progress toward a NVIDIA HBM3E or HBM4 qualification — will shadow the release and influence the multiple at which consensus underwrites the full-year estimate.

**H2 2026 — NVIDIA Rubin platform supply commitment.** NVIDIA's Rubin architecture, announced at GTC 2024 as the Blackwell successor, is the singular demand anchor for HBM4 volume in the forward window. Rubin GPUs are expected to require higher per-stack bandwidth than HBM3E, implying a further ASP step-up for the qualified supplier. DigiTimes and Reuters supply-chain reporting through Q1 2026 indicated SK Hynix remained the primary qualification partner for Rubin-generation HBM, consistent with the Blackwell-era pattern. A formal supply-framework confirmation — more likely to surface in earnings commentary or a press release than in an SEC filing — is the most consequential positive catalyst in the twelve-month window.

**H2 2026 — Indiana advanced-packaging groundbreaking.** SK Hynix's planned US HBM advanced-packaging facility in Indiana, announced with initial investment guidance of approximately USD 3.87 billion, is expected to move toward formal groundbreaking in H2 2026. A groundbreaking event paired with US Department of Commerce grant confirmation under the CHIPS and Science Act would be incrementally positive for the geopolitical risk-management narrative. The more consequential long-term signal is whether US-sited capacity attracts hyperscaler co-investment or long-term offtake commitments that structurally reduce cycle exposure.

**Late October 2026 — Q3 2026 earnings.** The third-quarter print is the definitive HBM4 ramp confirmation. Buy-side consensus at the snapshot date assumed H2 2026 would be the period when HBM4 volume crossed 50 per cent of total HBM shipped. If confirmed, the Q3 margin structure establishes the new baseline for 2027 modelling. A concurrent Solidigm gross margin disclosure will indicate whether the now-fully-consolidated ex-Intel NAND subsidiary has crossed into sustained positive contribution territory.

**Late January 2027 — Q4 2026 and full-year 2026 earnings.** The annual close sets consensus entry points for fiscal 2027. Management guidance on HBM4 ASP trajectory, the pace of conventional DRAM-to-HBM capacity reallocation, and any commentary on Samsung's competitive posture will be the principal re-rating inputs heading into the first half of 2027.

## Consensus Estimates

Sell-side consensus aggregated across Bloomberg and FactSet coverage available at the 23 May 2026 snapshot coalesced around the following operating profile. SK Hynix reports operating profit as the primary earnings metric; KRX 000660 KS shares are priced on price-to-book and EV/operating-profit multiples calibrated to the memory cycle, with the HBM premium stretching upward the multiple the market historically awarded at cycle peaks.

| ==Q1 2026 Actual== | ==52.58== | ==~200%== | ==37.61== | ==71.5%== |
| Q2 2026E | ~~18.3 – 19.8~~ ==52 – 56== | ~~48–56%~~ ==~90–110%== | ~~5.9 – 6.7~~ ==36 – 40== | ~~32–34%~~ ==68–72%== |
| Q3 2026E | ~~19.8 – 21.5~~ ==54 – 58== | ~~38–46%~~ ==~75–95%== | ~~6.5 – 7.5~~ ==37 – 42== | ~~33–35%~~ ==68–72%== |

| FY2026E | ~~76.0 – 83.0~~ ==213 – 226== | ~~+15–25%~~ ==+60–80%== | ~~24.5 – 29.0~~ ==148 – 162== | ~~31–35%~~ ==69–72%== |
